American lawyer and statesman, 16th president of the United States (1861–65). Born in a one-room log cabin in [[Kentucky]], he grew up on the frontier in Kentucky, Indiana, and [[Illinois]] and was largely self-educated. He became a lawyer, Illinois state legislator, and a one-term U.S. representative. Angered by the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which opened territories to slavery, he became a leader of the new [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and won national attention in the 1858 Senate campaign debates with Stephen A. Douglas.

Lincoln won the 1860 presidential election as the first Republican president, and most slave states began to secede. A month after he took office, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, beginning the [[American Civil War]] against the Confederate States. He closely supervised Union strategy. In April 1861 he suspended the writ of [[Habeas corpus|habeas corpus]]; Chief Justice Roger Taney held in *Ex parte Merryman* that only Congress could do so. Critics, then and later, saw his expansion of executive power as overreach, while supporters regarded it as necessary to save the Union. The war claimed over 620,000 lives.

On January 1, 1863, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring slaves in states "in rebellion" free; it was a war measure and did not cover Union border states. On November 19, 1863, he delivered the [[Gettysburg Address]]. He promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865. Re-elected in 1864, he favored a lenient Reconstruction.

On April 14, 1865, five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln was shot by [[John Wilkes Booth]] at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C., and died the next day, the first U.S. president to be assassinated. He is ranked in popular and scholarly polls among the greatest American presidents.

Hormone and medication, also known as epinephrine. Normally produced by the [[Adrenal gland|adrenal glands]] and a small number of neurons in the medulla oblongata, it plays an essential role in the fight-or-flight response, increasing blood flow to muscles, increasing [[Heart|heart]] output by acting on the SA node, dilating the pupils and raising [[Blood sugar level|blood sugar]]. It binds to alpha and beta receptors. As a medication, it treats anaphylaxis, [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]] and superficial bleeding, and inhaled adrenaline may ease croup. It can be used for [[Asthma|asthma]] when other treatments are not effective, and it lowers intraocular pressure in open-angle [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]] by increasing outflow of aqueous humor. Common side effects include shakiness, [[Anxiety|anxiety]] and sweating. The adrenal medulla contributes over 90% of circulating adrenaline, and a small number of neurons use it as a [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]].

Fully grown animal; in humans, a person who has attained legal and social independence. Biologically, an adult is an organism that has reached sexual maturity and is capable of reproduction. Historically and across cultures, human adulthood was determined chiefly by the onset of [[Puberty|puberty]], and the passage from child to adult was often marked by a coming-of-age test or ceremony. A person may be physically mature by about age 15 or 16 yet not be an adult in law until a later age.

Legally, an adult has reached the age of majority, when parents lose their rights and responsibilities regarding the person. The typical age is 18, although it varies by country, and in some places is 20 or 21. The age of majority may be set separately from the minimum ages for contracts, [[Marriage|marriage]], [[Voting|voting]], employment, military service, [[Firearm|firearms]], driving, alcohol, smoking, gambling, and other activities. In the U.S., for example, one cannot vote or join the armed forces until 18, and many legal and financial responsibilities begin at 21. Most modern societies set legal adulthood by age alone, without requiring a demonstration of maturity.

Definitions of adulthood are often inconsistent. A person may be biologically adult and behave maturely but still be treated as a child under the law, while another may be legally an adult yet lack maturity and responsibility. Media claims since 2005 that the brain reaches full maturity at age 25 rest on a 2004–05 imaging study of participants no older than 21; later studies show prefrontal cortex maturation continuing past age 30. Whether any single age of full mental maturity exists remains debated.

Fixed-wing aircraft propelled by a jet engine, propeller or rocket engine. The [[Wright brothers]]’ Wright Flyer, flown in 1903, is recognized as “the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight.” George Cayley set out the concept of the modern airplane in 1799. The German Heinkel He 178 was the first jet aircraft, in 1939, and the [[De Havilland Comet]], introduced in 1952, was the first jet airliner. The [[Boeing 707]] was in commercial service from 1958 to 2019. Commercial aviation transports more than four billion passengers a year. In American English the aircraft is called an airplane; in most of the Commonwealth it is an aeroplane.

Slovak communist statesman, de facto leader of Czechoslovakia (1968–69). As First Secretary of the Communist Party from January 1968, Dubček led the [[Prague Spring]] reforms, a program of cultural and economic liberalization known by the slogan "socialism with a human face." In August 1968 half a million Soviet-led [[Warsaw Pact]] troops invaded Czechoslovakia, reversing the reforms. Dubček was forced to resign in April 1969 and was expelled from the Communist Party in 1970. During the 1989 Velvet Revolution he served as chairman of the federal assembly and contended for the presidency with [[Václav Havel]]. The [[European Parliament]] awarded him the Sakharov Prize that year.

Children's novel by [[Lewis Carroll|Lewis Carroll]], published in 1865. Its heroine, Alice, falls through a rabbit hole into a world of anthropomorphic creatures, an example of literary nonsense. The book's [[Fantasy|fantasy]] and its play with [[Logic|logic]] gave it lasting appeal to adults as well as children. John Tenniel provided 42 wood-engraved illustrations for the original edition. Carroll first told the story on July 4, 1862, during a boat trip with the daughters of his friend Henry Liddell, and later wrote out the manuscript, now held by the [[British Library|British Library]]. The novel is credited with helping end an era of didacticism in [[Children's literature|children's literature]]. It has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages. Its legacy includes adaptations for film, ballet, [[Opera|opera]] and [[Musical theatre|musical theater]]. Carroll published the sequel *Through the Looking-Glass* in 1871.

Natural history museum on the Upper West Side of [[Manhattan]], New York City. The naturalist Albert S. Bickmore proposed the museum in 1861. It opened in [[Central Park]]'s Arsenal on May 22, 1871, and its first purpose-built structure in Theodore Roosevelt Park opened on December 22, 1877. The complex comprises 21 interconnected buildings with 45 permanent exhibition halls, a planetarium and a library. Its collections contain about 32 million specimens and artifacts, only a small fraction of which can be displayed at any time. The museum has a full-time scientific staff of 225, sponsors over 120 special field expeditions each year and averages about five million visits annually.

Bronze Age civilization along the lower [[Nile]] in northeastern Africa, and a cradle of civilization.

It emerged around 3150 BC (by conventional chronology), when Upper and Lower Egypt were united by Menes, whom most Egyptologists believe to be the same person as [[Narmer]]. Its history comprised stable kingdoms, the Old, Middle, and New, separated by Intermediate Periods of instability. The New Kingdom was the pinnacle of Egyptian power, extending its rule over much of [[Nubia]] and a considerable portion of the [[Levant]]. Egypt then slowly declined and was invaded or conquered by the Hyksos, Kushites, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. The end of ancient Egypt is variously placed at 332 BC, during the wars of [[Alexander the Great]], or at 30 BC, when the Greek-ruled [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]] fell to Rome.

Success rested on the Nile's predictable flooding and controlled irrigation, which produced surplus crops and supported dense population. A bureaucracy of scribes, religious leaders, and administrators served the [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]], who was believed to embody the god Horus on earth. Predynastic cultures with firm control of agriculture and animal husbandry had developed by about 5500 BC; the Naqada culture grew over about 1,000 years from small farming communities into a powerful civilization.

Achievements include quarrying, surveying, and construction techniques behind monumental pyramids, temples, and obelisks; mathematics, as in the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus; medicine; irrigation; the first known planked boats; faience and glass technology; and the earliest known peace treaty, with the Hittite Empire. Religion centered on preparation for the afterlife through mummification. Egyptian art and architecture were widely copied, and its ruins inspired travelers and writers for millennia.

Set of changing styles of building in ancient Egypt, most of whose surviving examples are religious and funerary structures. Because wood was scarce, the main materials were sun-dried mud brick and stone, chiefly limestone, with sandstone and granite used in considerable quantities. From the Old Kingdom onward stone was generally reserved for tombs and temples, while brick was used for palaces, fortresses and town walls. Monumental buildings used post-and-lintel construction, with thick sloping walls and closely spaced [[Column|columns]], and many were aligned astronomically. Although the [[Arch]] was developed in the fourth dynasty, monumental buildings did not adopt it. Column capitals were carved to resemble plants such as the [[Papyrus|papyrus]], and walls bore painted carvings. The best-known examples are the [[Pyramid|pyramids]] and the [[Sphinx]]. The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak, built by [[Ramesses II]], has columns up to 20 meters high. Egyptian motifs later influenced architecture elsewhere, first in the Greek Orientalizing period and again in 19th-century Egyptomania.

Russian and Soviet poet, born Anna Andreyevna Gorenko. She was born in a resort suburb of the [[Black Sea]] port of Odessa, then in the [[Russian Empire]] and now in [[Ukraine]]. Her style, marked by economy and emotional restraint, was strikingly original. Her cycle *Requiem* (1935–40) is about the Stalinist terror. Her work was condemned and censored by Stalinist authorities, and she chose not to emigrate, remaining in the [[Soviet Union]] as a witness to events around her. Her first husband, Nikolai Gumilev, was executed by the Cheka, and her son Lev Gumilev and her common-law husband Nikolay Punin spent many years in the [[Gulag]], where Punin died. Her early work (1912–25) and later work (from about 1936) were divided by a decade of reduced literary output. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1965 and 1966.

Brazilian composer and musician, also known as Tom Jobim, and a pioneer of [[Bossa nova|bossa nova]]. He merged [[Samba|samba]] with cool jazz in the 1960s. His song [[The Girl from Ipanema|“Garota de Ipanema”]] has been recorded over 240 times by other artists and is believed to be one of the most recorded popular songs in history. The 1964 album *Getz/Gilberto*, which featured several of his compositions, won [[Grammy Awards]] including Album of the Year, the first jazz record to do so. His 1967 album with [[Frank Sinatra]] was nominated for Album of the Year in 1968.

Willful killing, by sudden or secret attack, of a prominent or important person, typically for political, social or ideological reasons.

Assassinations may be ordered by individuals or organizations and carried out by the orderers themselves or by hired accomplices. Assassination is one of the oldest tools of power politics. The Egyptian pharaoh Teti, of the 23rd century BC, is thought to be the earliest known victim. *The Art of War*, a 5th-century BC Chinese military treatise, mentions assassination tactics.

The word *assassin* is believed to derive from *hashshashin*, the name of a group of Nizari Ismailis known as the [[Order of Assassins]], who were active in the Near East from the 11th to the 13th centuries. Notable victims include [[Philip II of Macedon]], father of [[Alexander the Great]], and [[Julius Caesar]]. [[Chanakya]] wrote about assassinations in his political treatise [[Arthashastra]], and his student [[Chandragupta Maurya]], founder of the [[Maurya Empire]], later used them against enemies.

Two-player [[Board game|board game]] played with counters and dice. It is the most widespread Western member of the tables family, whose ancestors date back at least 1,600 years. Each player has 15 pieces, traditionally called men, which move along 24 points according to the roll of two dice. The objective is to move all of one's pieces around the board and bear them off first. Removing all pieces while the opponent is still far behind earns a triple win, known as a backgammon. The game combines strategy with luck, and a doubling cube lets players raise the stakes during play. The earliest record of backgammon itself dates to 17th-century England, where it descended from the 16th-century game of Irish.

Capital city of West Java province, [[Indonesia]]. Located on the western highland of [[Java]], Bandung lies in a river basin surrounded by volcanic mountains that provided a natural defense, a reason the [[Dutch East Indies]] government planned to move the capital from Batavia (modern-day Jakarta). The Dutch established tea plantations in the mountains in the 18th century, and in 1906 the Dutch population won a municipal government. The city became a resort for Europeans, and the shops selling fashion from Paris earned it the nickname Parijs van Java. After Indonesian independence in 1945 it urbanized rapidly, facing problems with waste, floods and traffic. The first Asian-African Conference, the Bandung Conference, was hosted there by President [[Sukarno]] in 1955. The city joined the [[UNESCO]] Creative Cities Network in 2015, and it is Indonesia's major technology center.

Ranged weapon system consisting of an elastic bow and long-shafted projectiles, the arrows. Humans used bows for [[Hunting|hunting]] and aggression long before recorded history. They were important weapons of war from ancient history until the [[Early modern period|early modern period]], when [[Firearm|firearms]] made them increasingly obsolete. The earliest direct evidence of bow use dates to about 64,000 years ago at Sibudu Cave in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Bows are now used mainly for sport and hunting. [[Archery]] is the art of shooting arrows with a bow, and a bowyer is someone who makes bows.

Extensive region covering most of eastern, southern and central [[Brazil]]. It covers some 4,500,000 km² (1,930,511 sq mi), approximately half of the country's land area. The vast majority of Brazil's population (203,062,512 in the 2022 census) lives in the highlands or on the narrow coastal region beside them. Ancient [[Basalt|basaltic]] lava flows formed much of the region, which has no seismic or volcanic activity today. [[Erosion]] has shaped it into sedimentary deposits and worn-down mountains. Its diversity includes several [[Biome|biomes]], varied climates, many [[Soil|soil]] types and thousands of animal and plant species. The highlands are usually divided into the Atlantic Plateau along the eastern coast, the Southern Plateau and the Central Plateau, where about 85% of the land was once covered by [[Cerrado]] vegetation. The highest point is Pico da Bandeira, 2,891 m (9,485 ft), in the Serra do Caparaó.

Widespread, common species of [[Rat|rat]], also called the common rat, sewer rat or Norway rat. One of the largest muroids, it is brown or gray, up to 28 cm long, and weighs 140 to 500 g. It is thought to have originated in northern China and has spread to all continents except [[Antarctica]]. It is the dominant rat in [[Europe]] and much of [[North America]], and it lives wherever humans live, particularly in cities. Omnivorous and fast-breeding, it can carry several human diseases. Selective breeding produced the fancy rat and the laboratory rat, a [[Model organism|model organism]] in biological research. Despite its name, it did not originate in Norway.

Large terrestrial [[Bird|bird]] of the family Otididae, including floricans and korhaans. Bustards live mainly in dry grassland and [[Steppe|steppe]] regions, range from 40 to 150 cm in length, and 26 species are currently recognized. They are omnivorous, eating seeds, leaves, fruit, small [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] and [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]]. The kori bustard and great bustard (*Otis tarda*) are frequently cited as the world's heaviest flying birds. In most species males are substantially larger than females, while in the floricans the female is slightly larger. Bustards nest on the ground, and most prefer to run or walk rather than fly.

Country in Southeast Asia, officially the Kingdom of Cambodia, with a population of about 17.6 million as of 2024, predominantly ethnic Khmer. Its capital and largest city is [[Phnom Penh]]. The [[Khmer Empire]] (9th to 15th centuries) built [[Angkor Wat]], and Cambodia was a French protectorate from 1863 until independence in 1953. The [[Khmer Rouge]] regime carried out the [[Cambodian genocide]] from 1975 to 1979, and a later Vietnamese invasion ousted it. UN-supervised elections in 1993 restored a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]]. The Cambodian People's Party has dominated politics, and agriculture remains the largest economic sector, with growth in garments, tourism and construction.

Systematic persecution and killing of Cambodian citizens by the [[Khmer Rouge]] regime, 1975–79. Led by [[Pol Pot]], the Communist Party of Kampuchea emptied the cities and forced people into labor camps, where mass executions, forced labor, starvation and disease were rampant. Approximately 1.5 to 2 million people died, or 20% to 25% of the 1975 population, including ethnic minorities such as the Cham. China supplied at least 90% of the Khmer Rouge's foreign aid, and the [[Chinese Communist Party]] led by [[Mao Zedong]] supported the movement. A Vietnamese invasion toppled the regime in 1978. In 2019 the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia found Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan guilty of crimes against humanity and genocide, and both were sentenced to life imprisonment.

Even-toed ungulate in the genus *Camelus*, with fatty humps on its back, long domesticated for transport, milk, meat and fiber. There are three surviving species: the one-humped [[Dromedary]] and the two-humped [[Bactrian camel]], as well as the wild Bactrian camel, a distinct species that is endangered with around 1,000 individuals. Camels are adapted to desert habitats and are vital working animals that carry passengers and cargo. The wider family Camelidae includes the [[Llama|llama]], [[Alpaca|alpaca]], guanaco and vicuña. Camelids originated in North America during the [[Eocene]]; the ancestor of modern camels crossed into Asia during the late [[Miocene]], about 6 million years ago.

Geologic shield of exposed Precambrian igneous and high-grade metamorphic rock, centered on [[Hudson Bay]] in eastern and central [[Canada]]. It forms the [[North America|North American]] craton, the ancient geologic core of the continent, and its exposed area covers about 8,000,000 sq km (3,100,000 sq mi). Mountains once rose about 12,000 m (39,000 ft) before erosion reduced the region to low relief over some 500 million years. Its rocks date from 2.5 to 4.2 billion years. Glaciation has left a thin layer of soil, and many of Canada's major ore deposits are associated with greenstone belts. The shield also extends south into the northern United States.

Annual film festival in Cannes, France, considered the most prestigious in the world. The festival was conceived in 1938 as a rival to the Venice Film Festival, after [[Benito Mussolini]] and [[Adolf Hitler]] overruled jury decisions there. The first edition, postponed by [[World War II]], ran from September 20 to October 5, 1946, with films from 21 countries. Usually held in May at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès, the invitation-only festival previews new films of all genres, including [[Documentary film|documentaries]]. It was accredited by the FIAPF in 1951, the year it moved to spring to avoid competing with Venice. The top prize, the Palme d'Or, was introduced in 1955 and goes to the best feature film in official competition.

Economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit. Its elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets, and wage labor.

Analysts recognize forms including [[Laissez-faire|laissez-faire]], free-market, state, and welfare capitalism, which differ in the degree of free markets, public ownership, and regulation. Most existing economies are mixed economies combining free markets with state intervention and, in some cases, planning.

The modern form emerged from agrarianism in England and from mercantilist practices in European countries between the 16th and 18th centuries. [[Adam Smith]]'s *The Wealth of Nations* (1776) is cited as its intellectual foundation, and the [[Industrial Revolution]] of the 18th century made it the dominant mode of production, characterized by factory work and a complex division of labor. Through [[Globalization|globalization]] it spread across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. It was largely unregulated by the state in the 19th century, became more regulated after World War II through Keynesianism, and saw a return of less regulated capitalism termed [[Neoliberalism|neoliberalism]] from the 1980s.

The word *capitalist*, meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. The term *capitalism* in its modern sense is attributed to Louis Blanc in 1850 and [[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] in 1861; [[Karl Marx]] wrote of the capitalist mode of production in *Das Kapital* (1867).

Assessments differ. Supporters credit capitalist economies with sustained growth in GDP per capita and a decline in extreme poverty from over 90% of the world population in the 19th century to under 10%. Critics point to wealth disparities and recurrent business cycles, which defenders attribute to policy distortions such as subsidies and regulations favoring incumbents.

Class of iron–carbon [[Alloy|alloys]] containing more than 2% carbon and about 1–3% silicon. Its low melting temperature, good fluidity and wear resistance make it suitable for pipes, machine parts and [[Automotive industry|automotive]] parts such as cylinder heads and gearbox cases. Carbon, at 1.8 to 4% by weight, forms [[Graphite|graphite]] flakes in gray cast iron, which deflect cracks, or spherical nodules in ductile cast iron, which stop them. White cast iron holds its carbon as very hard but brittle cementite. Cast iron is brittle except for malleable grades and is notoriously difficult to weld. The earliest artifacts date to the 8th century BC in what is now [[Jiangsu]], [[China]]. In the 15th century it was used for cannons in Burgundy, France, and England. The first cast-iron bridge, the Iron Bridge in Shropshire, England, was built in the 1770s by Abraham Darby III.

Condition of fame and broad public recognition. Celebrity status can come from great wealth, participation in sports or entertainment, a political position, or a connection to another celebrity. Unlike *famous* or *notable*, the term usually implies a favorable public image. Historian Greg Jenner argues that the earliest celebrities lived in the early 1700s. In [[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greece]], athletes were welcomed home as heroes, and [[Julius Caesar]] appeared on a coin in his lifetime. [[Lord Byron]] became a celebrity in 1812 after publishing the first two cantos of *Childe Harold's Pilgrimage*. Juliet John has called [[Charles Dickens]] the first self-made global media star of the age of mass culture. In 1895, [[Oscar Wilde]] became the subject of "one of the first celebrity trials."

Substance composed of many identical molecules containing atoms from more than one [[Chemical element|chemical element]] held together by [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]]. A molecule consisting of atoms of only one element is therefore not a compound. A compound can be transformed into a different substance by a [[Chemical reaction|chemical reaction]], in which bonds between atoms may be broken, formed, or both.

Four major types are distinguished by how the atoms are bonded: molecular compounds, held together by covalent bonds; ionic compounds, held together by ionic bonds; intermetallic compounds, held together by metallic bonds; and coordination complexes, held together by coordinate covalent bonds. Non-stoichiometric compounds, whose proportions may be reproducible but are not integral, as in palladium hydride, PdHₓ (0.02 < x < 0.58), form a disputed marginal case.

A [[Chemical formula|chemical formula]] specifies the number of atoms of each element in a molecule of a compound, using standard chemical symbols with numerical subscripts. Water, for example, consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, with the formula H₂O. Many compounds have a unique CAS number assigned by the Chemical Abstracts Service. Globally, more than 350,000 chemical compounds (including mixtures of chemicals) have been registered for production and use.

The term "compound", with a meaning similar to the modern one, has been used at least since 1661, when [[Robert Boyle|Robert Boyle]]'s *The Sceptical Chymist* was published. In his *Logick* (1724), the English minister and logician Isaac Watts contrasted element with compound in clear, modern terms.

Fundamental individual rights and freedoms that governments pledge not to restrict without due process of law. They often include freedom of conscience, press, [[Freedom of religion|religion]], expression, and assembly, as well as personal security, [[Privacy|privacy]], equality before the law, a fair trial, and life. Scope differs by country, and property rights, reproductive rights, and civil marriage are disputed as civil liberties. Libertarians emphasize minimal government intervention in personal and economic affairs. [[John Stuart Mill]] argued in *On Liberty* for protecting individuals from government encroachment, and [[Friedrich Hayek]] warned in *The Road to Serfdom* against expanding state power. China's constitution guarantees civil liberties, but critics say subversion and state-secrets clauses are used to imprison critics of the [[Chinese Communist Party]].

City (pop., 2020: 372,624) in northeastern [[Ohio]], on the southern shore of [[Lake Erie]] and county seat of Cuyahoga County. Founded in 1796 near the mouth of the Cuyahoga River, it was named after General Moses Cleaveland and became a major commercial and industrial city by the late 19th century. It was among the top 10 largest U.S. cities by population for much of the 20th century. From the 1960s its economy slowed as manufacturing declined and suburbanization occurred. The city is a port connected to the Atlantic Ocean via the [[St. Lawrence Seaway]]. Its economy now relies on higher education, healthcare and financial services. Cultural institutions include the Cleveland Museum of Art, the Cleveland Orchestra and the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Long-term weather pattern of a region, typically averaged over 30 years.

More rigorously, climate is the mean and variability of meteorological variables over a span from months to millions of years. The variables most commonly measured are temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind, and precipitation. In a broader sense, climate is the state of the whole climate system: the [[Atmosphere|atmosphere]], hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere and the interactions among them. The word derives from Ancient Greek *klima*, 'inclination'. The standard averaging period of 30 years was defined by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), whose technical commission designated 1901–30 as the reference period for standard climate normals in 1934. The 1961–90 normals serve as the baseline reference period. The popular phrase "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get" summarizes the difference between climate and weather.

A location's climate is affected by its latitude, longitude, terrain, altitude, land use, and nearby bodies of water and their currents. Over historical time spans these determinants are nearly constant and change only over millions of years through processes such as [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. Others are more dynamic: [[Thermohaline circulation|thermohaline circulation]] of the ocean warms the northern Atlantic Ocean by 5 °C (9 °F) compared with other ocean basins, other ocean currents redistribute heat regionally, and vegetation affects heat absorption, water retention, and rainfall. Changes in atmospheric greenhouse gases, particularly [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and [[Methane|methane]], determine how much solar energy the planet retains.

Climates are classified by average and typical variables, most commonly temperature and precipitation. The most widely used scheme is the [[Köppen climate classification]], first developed in 1899, which was designed to identify climates associated with certain biomes. The Thornthwaite system, in use since 1948, adds evapotranspiration, and the Bergeron and Spatial Synoptic systems focus on the origin of air masses. Originally, climes were defined in Ancient Greece by a location's latitude. A common shortcoming of all such schemes is that they draw distinct boundaries, while real climates change gradually.

Paleoclimatology studies past climates. Because few direct observations exist before the 19th century, it relies on proxy evidence: sediments, ice cores, pollen, and rocks, as well as tree rings and coral. Climate models are mathematical models of past, present, and future climates.

Small migratory ground-nesting game bird of the pheasant family Phasianidae.

The common quail (*Coturnix coturnix*) breeds across the Palearctic and winters in Africa and southern India. Its characteristic call is three repeated chirps, and the male's song is a repetitive "wet-my-lips." It is notoriously hard to see, keeping hidden in crops and preferring to creep away rather than fly. Its diet consists of [[Seed|seeds]] and [[Insect|insects]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] described it in 1758 as *Tetrao coturnix*. The Japanese quail is now treated as a separate species, since crosses between the two show reduced fertility. Common quails are sometimes kept as [[Poultry|poultry]], and the IUCN classifies the species as least concern.

Political and economic ideology whose goal is a communist society: a classless order based on common ownership of the means of production, distribution, and exchange, with products allocated according to need. Such a society would have no private property or social classes and, ultimately, no money or state. The word derives from French *communisme*, from [[Latin]] *communis*, 'common'.

Communists often seek voluntary self-governance but disagree on the means. A libertarian socialist approach stresses revolutionary spontaneity and workers' self-management; an authoritarian socialist, party-driven approach aims to establish a socialist state expected to wither away. These share the analysis that under capitalism the proletariat, who sell their labor power, and the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, stand in an exploitative relationship that only social revolution can resolve.

Modern communism grew out of the 19th-century European socialist movement. In 1848 [[Karl Marx]] and Friedrich Engels offered a new definition in *The Communist Manifesto*. Communist governments espousing Marxism–Leninism came to power first in the Soviet Union with the 1917 Russian Revolution, and after World War II in Eastern Europe, Asia, and elsewhere.

For much of the 20th century more than one-third of the world's population lived under Communist governments, characterized by one-party rule, state control of the economy, and suppression of opposition. Supporters and critics assess the record differently: some regimes achieved rapid industrialization or literacy gains, while critics point to repression, forced labor, and famines. Mass killings under communist regimes and their mortality figures remain controversial and debated.

After the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991, many governments abolished Communist rule. Remaining Communist governments include China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, and Vietnam.

Group of woody, mostly evergreen [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperm]] plants that bear cones. There are over 600 living species. Each tree produces separate male and female cones, and the seeds are usually dispersed by wind. Conifers first appeared more than 300 million years ago in the [[Carboniferous|Carboniferous]] and dominated land plants during the Mesozoic, until [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] took over many ecosystems in the [[Cretaceous|Cretaceous]]. Conifers dominate the [[Taiga|taiga]] of the Northern Hemisphere, where conical shapes shed snow and waxy needle-shaped leaves limit water loss. The tallest living tree is a coast redwood, 116.07 m tall, and the oldest non-clonal living tree is a Great Basin bristlecone pine, 4,700 years old. As of 2025, 94 conifer species were listed as endangered. Conifers are of great economic value for timber and paper production.

Compulsory enlistment in national service, mainly [[Military|military]], enforced by law. Conscription dates to antiquity, but the modern system of near-universal conscription of young men began with the [[French Revolution]] in the 1790s. Most European nations later copied it in peacetime, with men serving one to eight years on active duty before transferring to the reserve. Conscription is controversial on grounds including conscientious objection, opposition to particular wars and sexism, since often only men are subject to the draft. [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]] became the first nations to conscript women on the same legal terms as men in the 2010s, and [[Denmark]] ruled in 2025 to implement a similar system. Many states that have abolished conscription keep the power to reinstate it in wartime. The [[United Kingdom]] abolished conscription in 1960, and it has not been enforced in the [[United States]] since 1973.

Choice and willingness to confront [[Pain|pain]], danger, uncertainty or intimidation, also called bravery or valor. Physical courage is bravery in the face of pain, hardship or death, while moral courage is the ability to act rightly despite popular opposition, shame or personal loss. The classical [[Virtue|virtue]] of fortitude, also translated as courage, includes perseverance and patience. Philosophers including [[Socrates]], [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] wrote on courage, and the Chinese text [[Tao Te Ching]] addresses both physical and moral courage. Professor Daniel Putman argues that courage involves deliberate choice in the face of fearful circumstances for the sake of a worthy goal, and that the balance of fear and confidence determines whether courage is distorted.

Idealized and heroic image of a leader, built through flattery and propaganda. Such an image is created through mass media, propaganda, staged spectacles, the arts, [[Patriotism|patriotism]], and government-organized rallies. It resembles apotheosis but uses modern social engineering, and it is usually established by the state or party in one-party states. Cults of personality often accompany totalitarian or authoritarian governments, though they also appear in some monarchies and liberal democracies. The most notorious examples arose in the 20th century, when mass media allowed leaders to project images to the masses, including those of [[Joseph Stalin]] and [[Mao Zedong]]. The [[Internet]] and social media have renewed the phenomenon in the 21st century. Critics argue that regimes construct such cults to avoid accountability, while proponents describe them as organic [[Charisma|charisma]].

Northern constellation on the plane of the [[Milky Way]], named for the Latinized Greek word for swan. It was among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer [[Ptolemy]] and remains one of the 88 modern constellations. It contains the Northern Cross asterism and Deneb, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. The constellation is also home to [[Cygnus X-1]], the first object widely held to be a [[Black hole|black hole]].

Israelite king and second monarch of the united Kingdom of Israel, according to the [[Hebrew Bible]]. In the biblical narrative, David is a shepherd and harpist who kills the Philistine [[Goliath]] and later rules first Judah and then all Israel. He conquers [[Jerusalem]] and makes it his capital. His reign includes adultery with Bathsheba, the death of her husband, and a rebellion led by his son Absalom. Denied permission to build God's temple, he names [[Solomon]] as his successor. He is portrayed as an ideal king and ancestor of the future [[Messiah|Messiah]], and is referenced in the [[New Testament]]. The [[Quran|Quran]] and [[Hadith|hadith]] describe him as an Israelite king and a prophet. Most knowledge of David comes from biblical literature, whose historicity has been extensively challenged, and his reign may have occurred around the 9th century BC.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata. Serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* from December 2003 to May 2006, it follows a high school student who finds a notebook in which writing a name causes that person's death. Light Yagami pursues a crime-free world under the alias Kira, while an elite police task force led by the detective L hunts him. A 37-episode [[Anime|anime]] series aired in 2006–07, and an American film was released on [[Netflix]] in 2017.

Electrical insulator that can be polarized by an applied electric field. Unlike a conductor, a dielectric has no loosely bound, free electrons to carry current. In an electric field its charges shift slightly from their equilibrium positions, producing an internal field that reduces the overall field. Dielectric properties govern the storage and dissipation of electric and magnetic energy, and they are important in electronics, optics and solid-state physics. A dielectric is the insulating material between the plates of a [[Capacitor|capacitor]], where polarization increases the capacitor's surface charge. The term was coined by William Whewell at the request of [[Michael Faraday]].

Country in the [[Horn of Africa]], on the [[Red Sea]] and the [[Gulf of Aden]]. It is bordered by [[Somalia]], [[Ethiopia]] and [[Eritrea]], and has an area of 23,200 km2. In antiquity the territory was part of the [[Land of Punt]]. It gained independence from France in 1977, after a referendum, and joined the [[United Nations]] in its first year. Its population was 1,066,809 at the census of May 20, 2024, the smallest in mainland Africa. French and Arabic are official languages, and about 94% of Djiboutians adhere to Islam. The country controls access between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean and serves as the principal maritime port for Ethiopia's imports and exports. It hosts several foreign military bases and the headquarters of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD).

Informal group of [[Beetle|beetles]] that feed on feces. They belong to the superfamily Scarabaeoidea but are not a single taxonomic group, so dung feeding has evolved more than once. The subfamily Scarabaeinae alone comprises more than 5,000 species. Many feed on the dung of [[Herbivore|herbivores]] and omnivores, and they occur on every continent except [[Antarctica]]. In 1991 Ilkka Cambefort and Yves Hanski classified dung beetles as rollers, which shape dung into balls for food or brood, tunnelers, which bury dung where they find it, and dwellers, which live within dung. In the late 19th century Jean Henri Fabre showed that apparent helpers of a rolling beetle were waiting to steal its food. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] revered dung-rolling as the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky.

Global climate phenomenon of fluctuating sea surface temperatures over the tropical [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]]. Its warming phase is called El Niño and its cooling phase La Niña, and the Southern Oscillation is the accompanying shift in [[Atmospheric pressure|surface air pressure]]. The phases recur irregularly about every two to seven years and are not easily predictable. El Niño causes short-term spikes in global average surface temperature, lasting about one year, while La Niña causes short-term cooling. The phenomenon disrupts weather across the [[Tropics|tropics]] and beyond, bringing intense storms to some places and droughts to others. The countries most affected are developing countries bordering the Pacific that depend on agriculture and fishing. The term was first recorded in a climate context in 1892, when Captain Camilo Carrillo reported to a geographical congress in [[Lima]] that Peruvian sailors had named the warm current after the Christ Child, as it typically appeared around [[Christmas]].

Distribution of electrons among the atomic or molecular orbitals of an atom or molecule. For example, the configuration of neon is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, meaning that the 1s, 2s and 2p subshells hold two, two and six electrons. Each electron is described by four quantum numbers, and the [[Pauli exclusion principle]] states that no two electrons can share the same set of four. The Aufbau principle dictates that electrons fill orbitals from the lowest energy level upward, producing the ground state, the lowest-energy configuration. An electron can move to a different configuration by emitting or absorbing a photon. Electron configuration explains the structure of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]], the nature of [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]] and molecular geometry, and the behavior of lasers and semiconductors.

Queen of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms (r. 1952–2022). She succeeded her father, [[George VI|George VI]], in February 1952 and was crowned in [[Westminster Abbey|Westminster Abbey]] in 1953. Her reign of 70 years and 214 days was the longest of any British monarch. As a constitutional monarch she reigned through the decolonization of Africa, the [[The Troubles|Troubles]] in Northern Ireland, and the United Kingdom's accession to and withdrawal from the European Communities. She was advised by more than 170 prime ministers and met five popes and fourteen U.S. presidents. She died aged 96 at Balmoral Castle and was succeeded by her eldest son, [[Charles III|Charles III]].

American [[Jazz|jazz]] singer and songwriter, known for her purity of tone, diction and scat singing. She rose to national fame with the Chick Webb Orchestra, whose recording of the nursery rhyme "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" made her and Webb famous. After Webb died she took over the band, and in 1942 she began a solo career. With Verve Records she recorded influential interpretations of the Great American Songbook. Her partnerships with [[Louis Armstrong|Louis Armstrong]] and [[Duke Ellington|Duke Ellington]] produced songs including "Cheek to Cheek" and "Dream a Little Dream of Me." Her last public performance was in 1993. Her honors include the Presidential Medal of Freedom and multiple [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]].

Founding emperor of the [[Song dynasty]] of China (r. 960–976). Personal name Zhao Kuangyin. A distinguished general of the Later Zhou dynasty, he came to power after staging a [[Coup d'état|coup]] and forcing the last Later Zhou ruler to abdicate. He conquered Southern Tang, Later Shu, Southern Han and Jingnan, reunifying most of China proper. To strengthen his control he reduced the power of military generals and relied on civilian officials. He was succeeded by his younger brother, Zhao Kuangyi (Emperor Taizong).

Study of the distribution and determinants of disease and other health conditions in human populations. It is a cornerstone of [[Public health|public health]], identifying risk factors for disease and targets for [[Preventive healthcare|preventive healthcare]], and it shapes policy. Major areas include disease causation, transmission, outbreak investigation, surveillance and the comparison of treatment effects in clinical trials. Epidemiologists rely on biology, [[Statistics|statistics]], the social sciences and engineering. In 1854 [[John Snow]] traced a [[Cholera|cholera]] outbreak in London's Broad Street to a contaminated water pump, demonstrating waterborne transmission. Descriptive studies characterize cases by time, place and person, while analytic studies test hypotheses through cohort, case-control and randomized controlled trials. The term appears to have been first used to describe the study of epidemics in 1802 by the Spanish physician Joaquín de Villalba.

Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer. Shackleton first went to Antarctica in 1901 as third officer on [[Robert Falcon Scott]]'s Discovery expedition. On the Nimrod expedition (1907–1909), his party set a Farthest South record of 88°23′ S, only 97 geographical miles from the [[South Pole]]. On the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, his ship *Endurance* was trapped in pack ice in the [[Weddell Sea]] and sank in 1915. The crew camped on the ice, then reached Elephant Island by lifeboat, and Shackleton sailed 720 nautical miles to South Georgia to bring rescue. He died of a heart attack while his ship was moored at South Georgia on a 1921 expedition. Later rediscovered as a model of leadership in extreme circumstances, he was voted eleventh in a [[BBC]] poll of the 100 Greatest Britons.

Category of steroid sex hormones that regulate the female reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics. The three major endogenous estrogens are estrone (E1), estradiol (E2) and estriol (E3); estradiol is the most potent and prevalent. Estetrol (E4) is produced only during pregnancy. Estrogens bind to estrogen receptors inside cells, which modulate the expression of many genes, and also activate membrane receptors such as GPER. They are synthesized from [[Testosterone|testosterone]] and other androgens by the [[Enzyme|enzyme]] aromatase. Estrogens are used as medications in [[Menopause|menopausal]] hormone therapy and hormonal birth control. Synthetic and natural estrogens found in the environment, known as xenoestrogens, are among the endocrine-disrupting compounds that can cause reproductive dysfunction in wildlife and humans. In both sexes, circulating levels of estrogen are lower than those of androgens.

Efficient [[Algorithm|algorithm]] for computing the greatest common divisor of two [[Integer|integers]]. Named after the ancient Greek mathematician [[Euclid]], who described it in his *Elements* (c. 300 BC), it is one of the oldest algorithms in common use. It rests on the principle that the greatest common divisor does not change if the larger number is replaced by its remainder when divided by the smaller. Repeating this produces smaller pairs until the remainder is zero. The number of steps never exceeds five times the number of base-10 digits of the smaller integer, a result proven by Gabriel Lamé in 1844 that marks the beginning of [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity theory]]. The algorithm reduces fractions, performs division in [[Modular arithmetic|modular arithmetic]], helps solve [[Diophantine equation|Diophantine equations]] and forms part of the cryptographic protocols that secure the [[Internet]].

Mathematical formula in [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]] linking the trigonometric functions with the complex exponential function. For any real number x, eⁱˣ = cos x + i sin x, where e is the base of the natural logarithm and i is the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]]. [[Leonhard Euler]] presented it in his 1748 treatise *Introductio in analysin infinitorum*. The formula remains valid when x is complex, and it is used throughout mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering. Physicist [[Richard Feynman]] called it "our jewel" and "the most remarkable formula in mathematics". Setting x = π yields [[Euler's identity]].

Family that extends beyond the [[Nuclear family|nuclear family]] to include aunts, uncles, grandparents, cousins and other relatives, living nearby or in the same household. A stem family, first discussed by Frédéric Le Play, has parents living with one child, that child's spouse and their children, while other children leave or remain unmarried. Stem families are associated with unequal inheritance in [[Japan|Japan]] and [[Korea|Korea]], while in traditional [[Romania|Romania]] and northeastern [[Thailand|Thailand]] the child who cares for the parents usually receives the house. Extended families often form support networks even when living apart, and [[Facebook|Facebook]] is commonly used to maintain these ties. An estimated 49 million Americans, or 16.1 percent of the total population, live in homes with three or more generations, up from 42 million in 2000.

North American theater of the [[Seven Years' War]], fought from 1754 to 1763 between Great Britain and France with their Indigenous allies. Historians generally treat it as part of the global Seven Years' War, but in the United States it is often viewed as a distinct conflict. It began in May 1754 at the Battle of Jumonville Glen, when Virginia militia led by [[George Washington]] ambushed a French patrol. Edward Braddock's expedition was defeated at the Battle of the Monongahela in 1755, and Britain captured [[Quebec]] in 1759 and Montreal the following year. The Treaty of Paris in 1763 transferred France's Canadian possessions and its claims east of the [[Mississippi River]] to Britain. Spain received French Louisiana west of the river, and France retained only [[Saint Pierre and Miquelon]].

German philosopher and classical philologist. In 1869, at age 24, he became professor of classical philology at the University of [[Basel]], but ill health forced him to resign in 1879. He then worked as an independent writer, moving between Switzerland, Italy and southern France. His mature works include *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, *Beyond Good and Evil* and *On the Genealogy of Morality*. He critiqued objective truth in favor of perspectivism, attacked Christian morality as a slave morality, and developed the concepts of the *Übermensch*, the will to power and eternal return. After a neurological collapse in 1889 he was cared for by his mother and then his sister. Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche edited his unpublished writings to fit her ultranationalist ideology, and his work became associated with fascism and [[Nazism]]. Twentieth-century scholars such as Walter Kaufmann defended his original views, and his influence spans [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and [[Postmodernism|postmodernism]].

Austrian-born film director. Lang worked in Germany and later in the United States. His science-fiction film *Metropolis* (1927) and the early film noir *M* (1931) are among his best-known works. His 1929 film *Woman in the Moon* showcased a multi-stage [[Rocket|rocket]] and pioneered the rocket-launch countdown clock. Born in [[Vienna]], he served in the Austrian army in [[World War I]]. Lang fled Nazi Germany in 1933 after a meeting with Propaganda Minister [[Joseph Goebbels|Joseph Goebbels]], who had offered him a position in the state film industry. In Hollywood he directed *Fury* (1936) and *The Big Heat* (1953). He became a naturalized United States citizen in 1939 and returned to Germany in the late 1950s.

Literary works written in the German language. Medieval works include the *Hildebrandslied*, the heroic epic *Heliand*, and courtly epics such as the *Nibelungenlied*. [[Martin Luther]]'s Bible translation, published between 1522 and 1534, helped standardize Modern High German. Modern German literature began with Enlightenment authors such as Herder, and Goethe's best-selling *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) ended the Sensibility movement. [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]] and [[Friedrich Schiller|Schiller]] led the Sturm und Drang and Weimar Classicism movements, and [[Romanticism|German Romanticism]] dominated the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Under the Nazi regime, some authors went into exile and others practiced "internal emigration". German-language authors have won the Nobel Prize in Literature 14 times, including [[Thomas Mann]] and [[Hermann Hesse]].

Common high-grade [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]] with a banded texture. It forms when [[Igneous rock|igneous]] or [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rocks]] are subjected to high temperature and pressure, ranging from 2 to 15 kbar, sometimes more, and temperatures over 300 °C. Gneiss nearly always shows alternating darker and lighter bands and lacks a distinct cleavage. The darker bands contain more mafic minerals, rich in magnesium and iron, while the lighter bands contain more felsic minerals such as [[Feldspar|feldspar]] and [[Quartz|quartz]]. Gneisses are common in the ancient crust of continental shields, and some of the oldest rocks on Earth are gneisses, such as the Acasta Gneiss.

[[Search engine]] operated by [[Google]]. Launched in 1998 as the company's first product, it was mostly developed by [[Larry Page]] and [[Sergey Brin]]. Users enter keywords into a search box, and results are indexed by PageRank and other proprietary [[Algorithm|algorithms]]. Since the 2020s it has been integrated with [[Generative AI|generative AI]] features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode. Google.com is the most-visited [[Website|website]] in the world, with an estimated 90% share of the global search-engine market as of 2026. In 2024 a U.S. federal court ruled in *United States v. Google LLC* that the company held an illegal [[Monopoly|monopoly]] over internet search and search advertising.

Category of plant tissues that are neither dermal nor [[Vascular tissue|vascular]], forming the bulk of the plant body. Ground tissue is one of three main tissue systems, alongside the protective and vascular systems, and it provides structural support, storage, metabolic activity and [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Its cells are classified by their [[Cell wall|cell walls]]. Parenchyma cells have thin primary walls, usually remain alive at maturity and form the filler tissue of soft parts; they store starch in roots, [[Potato|tubers]] and [[Cereal|cereal]] seed endosperm, and their large central [[Vacuole|vacuoles]] store water and ions. Collenchyma cells provide extra support in regions of new growth. Sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified walls, often die at maturity and provide the main structural support. Aerenchyma, with large air cavities, helps aquatic plants float.

Large 1937 anti-war [[Oil painting|oil painting]] by Spanish artist [[Pablo Picasso|Pablo Picasso]]. Picasso painted *Guernica* in Paris in response to the April 26, 1937, bombing of the Basque town of Guernica by aircraft of [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]]'s Condor Legion and the fascist government of Italy, during the [[Spanish Civil War|Spanish Civil War]]. The gray, black and white canvas, 3.49 m by 7.76 m, shows grieving women, a gored horse, a bull, a dead dove, a dead baby and flames. Many art critics regard it as the most moving and powerful anti-war painting in history. It was shown at the Spanish pavilion of the 1937 Paris International Exposition and then toured to raise funds for Spanish war relief. It is now housed in the Museo Reina Sofía in [[Madrid|Madrid]].

[[Sweden|King of Sweden]] (1611–1632), credited with raising Sweden to the rank of a great European power. Born in [[Stockholm]], he came to the throne at age 16, inheriting wars with Russia and Denmark–Norway and a dynastic struggle with his cousin [[Sigismund III Vasa]] of Poland. He is regarded as one of the greatest military commanders in modern history. He employed mobile artillery and aggressive tactics, and he is often called the father of modern warfare. He was the main figure in Swedish success in the [[Thirty Years' War]], winning the Battle of Breitenfeld in 1631, and he was killed at the Battle of Lützen the following year. He reformed administration, including parish registration, so that the government could tax and conscript more efficiently.

Nineteenth monarch of Goguryeo. He took the title Taewang, equivalent to "emperor", placing Goguryeo on equal standing with the imperial dynasties of China. Under him Goguryeo became one of the great powers of [[East Asia]]. In 396 he defeated Baekje, then the most powerful of the [[Three Kingdoms of Korea]], and captured its capital, Wiryeseong, in present-day [[Seoul]]. In 399 he dispatched 50,000 troops to aid Silla, which became a de facto protectorate. His western campaigns defeated the Xianbei of the Later Yan empire and conquered the Liaodong peninsula, and his conquests extended into [[Manchuria]] and [[Inner Mongolia]]. His achievements are recorded on the Gwanggaeto Stele, erected in 414 by his son Jangsu near the supposed site of his tomb in Ji'an, on the China–North Korea border. It is the largest engraved stele in the world.

Arabic term for what is permissible under [[Sharia|Islamic law]]. Although the term is often associated with dietary laws, particularly the slaughter of meat, halal also governs business and finance, such as the prohibition of usury (riba), and daily living. In the [[Quran|Quran]], halal is contrasted with [[Haram|haram]], meaning forbidden. Islam generally considers all food halal unless it is specifically prohibited in the Quran or [[Hadith|hadith]], and pork is the only meat that is categorically forbidden. Halal has grown into a global industry, with certification bodies serving the food, pharmaceutical, [[Cosmetics|cosmetic]] and financial sectors. The halal economy has grown especially in countries with large Muslim populations, such as Malaysia, Indonesia and the [[Middle East|Middle East]].

[[Capital city|Capital]] and second-most populous city of [[Vietnam]] (pop., 2023: 8,587,141). Hanoi covers 3,358.6 sq km and houses the National Assembly and the presidential palace. Founded in 1010 by the Lý dynasty emperor Lý Thái Tổ as Thăng Long, it was renamed Đông Kinh in 1428 and became Hanoi in 1831. It was the capital of [[French Indochina]] from 1902 to 1945 and became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam in 1976. Sites include the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the [[Ho Chi Minh]] Mausoleum and Hoàn Kiếm Lake. [[UNESCO]] designated Hanoi a City of Peace in 1999.

German-born British biochemist. Krebs was a pioneer in the study of [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]], the process by which cells extract energy from food and oxygen. With Kurt Henseleit, he discovered the urea cycle, the metabolic pathway for urea formation, while at Freiburg in 1932. He is best known for the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]], often called the Krebs cycle, which lets oxygen-respiring cells obtain far more ATP from food than [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]] can supply. That work earned him the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Nazi racial laws ended his career in Germany, and he settled in England, working at [[Oxford]] from 1954 until his retirement in 1967. He was knighted in 1958.

Romantic attraction, sexual attraction or sexual behavior between people of the opposite sex or gender. As a [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientation]], it is one of three main categories along with [[Bisexuality]] and [[Homosexuality]], and the term also refers to a sense of identity based on those attractions. Across cultures most people are heterosexual, and heterosexual activity is by far the most common type of sexual activity. It has mostly been viewed as the normative and most socially dominant form of sexual orientation. Scientists do not know the exact cause of sexual orientation, but they theorize that it results from a complex interplay of genetic, hormonal and environmental influences, and they favor biologically based theories. The term was coined alongside homosexual by Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1869.

Rail transport network using trains that run significantly faster than conventional trains on dedicated tracks. Lines are generally considered high-speed when built for at least 250 km/h (155 mph), or when upgraded lines run at least 200 km/h (125 mph). The first dedicated system, the Tōkaidō [[Shinkansen]] in [[Japan]], opened in October 1964; its streamlined nose gave the trains the nickname bullet train. European countries followed, starting with [[Italy]]'s Direttissima line and then [[France]], Germany and Spain. As of 2023, [[China]]'s network accounted for over two-thirds of the world's total. High-speed trains mostly run on standard gauge track. High-speed rail is the fastest and most efficient ground-based method of commercial transport, but its construction costs more than conventional rail and does not always offer an economic advantage.

Type of vector space that generalizes Euclidean space to any finite or infinite dimension. A Hilbert space has an inner product that allows length and angle to be measured, and it is complete, so that enough limits exist for the techniques of calculus. It was studied from the first decade of the 20th century by [[David Hilbert]], Erhard Schmidt and Frigyes Riesz, and it is indispensable in [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]], [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], Fourier analysis and ergodic theory. [[John von Neumann]] coined the term for the abstract concept. Examples include spaces of square-integrable functions and of sequences. Exact analogs of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] hold, and perpendicular projection onto a subspace is central to optimization. These methods helped establish [[Functional analysis|functional analysis]] as a fruitful field.

Human history of the Australian continent, from Aboriginal settlement to a multicultural federal democracy. The first ancestors of [[Aboriginal Australians]] arrived from Maritime Southeast Asia between 50,000 and 65,000 years ago, and their artistic and spiritual traditions are among the longest surviving in human history. Dutch navigators named the continent New Holland in the 17th century. In 1770 [[James Cook]] charted the east coast and claimed it for Great Britain. The First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove in January 1788 and established a penal colony. Disease, violence and dispossession reduced the Aboriginal population. Gold rushes and agriculture brought prosperity, and the six colonies voted to federate in 1901 as the Commonwealth of Australia. Australia fought in both world wars as part of the [[British Empire]] and became a long-standing ally of the United States through the [[Cold War]]. Post-war immigration from almost every country brought the population to more than 25.5 million by 2021, with 30 percent born overseas.

Development of the study and mapping of the Earth, from ancient Mesopotamian maps to an academic discipline. The word geography, from the Greek for Earth-writing, was first used by [[Eratosthenes]], but recognizable practices such as [[Cartography|cartography]] existed earlier. The oldest known world maps date to ancient [[Babylon]], and the best-known Babylonian map, the Imago Mundi of 600 BC, shows Babylon on the Euphrates surrounded by a circular landmass. The Greeks viewed [[Homer]] as the founder of geography, since the *Iliad* and *Odyssey* contain much geographical information. [[Thales of Miletus]] laid down astronomical and mathematical rules that allowed geography to be studied scientifically, and his successor Anaximander attempted the first scale map of the known world. [[Herodotus]]' *Histories* describes much of the known world, including Egypt, Scythia and Persia. Geography later became a distinct academic discipline.

Development of organized physical competition from prehistoric activity to modern professional sport. Sport had early links with warfare and entertainment, and competition was used to determine whether individuals were fit for military service. Cave paintings in France appear to depict sprinting in the Upper Paleolithic, and rock art in Egypt shows swimming and archery. Wrestlers are depicted on Sumerian stone slabs dated to around 3000 BC, and the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]] describes belt wrestling. Monuments at Beni Hasan dating to around 2000 BC show that wrestling, weightlifting, long jump, swimming and archery were well developed in [[Ancient Egypt]]. The first Olympic Games were recorded in 776 BC at Olympia, where they were held every four years until 393 AD. [[Pierre de Coubertin]]'s 1896 Olympic revival transformed sport into a global arena. In the 19th century [[Cricket]] and [[Association football]] gained standardized rules, enabling mass participation and commercialization.

Current geological epoch, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago. It follows the [[Last Glacial Period]] and, with the preceding [[Pleistocene]], forms the [[Quaternary]] period. The Holocene is an interglacial period equivalent to Marine Isotope Stage 1. Because it corresponds with the rapid growth and impact of the human species, it is often called the Age of Humans. Its ecosystems continue to be affected by the [[Holocene extinction]], largely of human causation. In July 2018 the International Union of Geological Sciences divided the epoch into three ages: the Greenlandian (11,700 to 8,200 years ago), the Northgrippian (8,200 to 4,200 years ago) and the Meghalayan (4,200 years ago to the present).

Playground game in which players toss a small marker into numbered squares and hop through the course. It is popular in many countries and can be played with several players or alone. The court is drawn in [[Chalk|chalk]] on pavement or scratched in dirt, usually as a series of linear [[Square|squares]] interspersed with pairs of side-by-side squares. Single squares are hopped on one foot and paired squares are straddled, and a turn ends if a player steps on a line, misses a square, or loses balance. The first player to complete one course for every numbered square wins. The origin of the game is unknown, and there is no evidence that it existed before the 16th century. The earliest English references date to the late 17th century, under names such as "scotch-hop". It is both a physical and cognitive [[Exercise|workout]].

Name given to several real and fictitious groups, most often the Bavarian Illuminati, an Enlightenment-era [[Secret society|secret society]]. Founded on 1 May 1776 in the Electorate of [[Bavaria]], it aimed to oppose superstition, religious influence over public life and abuses of state power by monarchs. Charles Theodore, Elector of Bavaria, outlawed it in 1784, 1785, 1787 and 1790, with the encouragement of the [[Catholic Church]]. Conservative critics later claimed that it continued underground and was responsible for the [[French Revolution]], though these links have not been substantiated. Later organizations alleged to continue it have been accused of conspiring to control world affairs.

Silvery-white post-transition metal; chemical element with symbol In and atomic number 49. It is one of the softest elements, so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and its properties are intermediate between those of [[Gallium]] and thallium. Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter discovered it in 1863 by spectroscopic methods and named it for the indigo-blue line in its spectrum. Indium is used mainly in [[Flat-panel display|flat-panel displays]] as indium tin oxide (ITO), a transparent conductive coating on glass, and in [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]], low-melting solders and blue and white LEDs. It is produced as a by-product of processing other metal ores, chiefly zinc sulfide ores. Indium has no biological role, and its compounds are toxic when inhaled or injected.

American-born dancer and choreographer, a pioneer of [[Modern dance|modern dance]]. Born and raised in California, she lived and danced in Western Europe, the United States, and Soviet Russia from the age of 22. Her natural, free movement contrasted with the rigidity of [[Ballet|ballet]], and she drew inspiration from Greek vase paintings and bas-reliefs in the [[British Museum]]. After working in Augustin Daly's company in [[New York City]], she grew disillusioned with the form and moved to London in 1898, performing in the drawing rooms of the wealthy. In 1902 Loie Fuller invited her to tour Europe. Despite mixed reactions from critics, she inspired visual artists, including [[Auguste Rodin]], to create works based on her. In 1910 she met the occultist [[Aleister Crowley]] at a party. She died in [[Nice]], France, when her scarf became entangled in the wheel and axle of the car in which she was traveling.

Canadian and New Zealand filmmaker and explorer. His films combine cutting-edge technology with classical filmmaking techniques and have grossed over $10 billion worldwide, making him the second-highest-grossing film director of all time. He has received three Academy Awards, for Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing for *Titanic* (1997). His earlier films include *The Terminator* (1984), *Aliens* (1986), and *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* (1991). In 2012 he became the first person to make a solo descent to the bottom of the [[Mariana Trench]], the deepest part of Earth's ocean, in the submersible *Deepsea Challenger*. A [[National Geographic]] explorer-in-residence, he has produced documentaries on deep-ocean exploration, and in 2010 [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world.

American actress. Woodward won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *The Three Faces of Eve* (1957), playing a woman with [[Dissociative identity disorder|dissociative identity disorder]]. She was married to [[Paul Newman]] for 50 years, until his death, and the two often worked together. Her mother named her after [[Joan Crawford]]. Woodward has won three Primetime Emmy Awards, a British Academy Film Award and three Golden Globe Awards. In 1990 she earned a bachelor's degree from Sarah Lawrence College at age 60, graduating alongside her daughter Clea. She is the oldest living Best Actress Oscar winner.

English heavy metal band formed in [[Birmingham]] in 1969. The band was a pioneer of the new wave of British heavy metal and an influence on speed, thrash and power metal. It struggled commercially until *British Steel* (1980) brought mainstream attention. [[The Guardian]] called *British Steel* the record that defines heavy metal. Rob Halford, who joined as vocalist in 1973, left in 1992 and returned in 2003. The band has sold over 50 million albums and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2022.

Marginal sea of the [[Arctic Ocean]] north of Siberia. It lies between the [[Barents Sea]] to the west, separated by the Kara Strait and [[Novaya Zemlya]], and the Laptev Sea to the east, separated by the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago. Roughly 1,450 km (900 mi) long and 970 km (600 mi) wide, it covers about 880,000 sq km (339,770 sq mi) and has a mean depth of 110 m (360 ft). The sea is ice-bound for all but two months of the year. Its main ports are Novy Port and Dikson, and it is an important [[Fishing|fishing]] ground. The East-Prinovozemelsky field, an extension of the West Siberian Oil Basin, contains significant undeveloped [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and natural gas. The name comes from the Kara River; *kara* may derive from a Nenets word meaning "hummocked ice" or a Turkic word meaning "black."

Capital and largest city of [[Tatarstan]], Russia. Kazan lies at the confluence of the [[Volga]] and Kazanka rivers and has a population of over 1.3 million. It was the capital of the [[Khanate of Kazan]], which [[Ivan the Terrible]] conquered in the 16th century, after which the city became part of the [[Tsardom of Russia]]. Pugachev's Rebellion (1773–75) seized and largely destroyed the city, which was rebuilt under [[Catherine the Great]]. In 1920 Kazan became capital of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, and after the Soviet Union dissolved it remained capital of Tatarstan. The Kazan Kremlin is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site, and the city hosted the 2013 Summer Universiade and the BRICS Games in 2024.

Disputed super-Earth exoplanet candidate orbiting the Sun-like star Kepler-452. Initial reports claimed it orbits within the inner edge of the habitable zone, and it is the only planet in its system discovered by the Kepler space telescope. Two later reports refuted the claim, but further work reestablished it. It lies about 1,800 light-years from Earth in the constellation [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]]. Its radius is around 1.63 times that of Earth, and it orbits at 1.04 AU with a period of roughly 385 days. It receives slightly more energy from its star than Earth and could experience a runaway greenhouse effect.

Colored ornamental variety of [[Carp|carp]], also called *nishikigoi* (brocaded carp). They are kept in outdoor ponds and water gardens. Systematic breeding for color and pattern began in Niigata, [[Japan]], in the early 19th century. Varieties are distinguished by coloration, patterning and scalation, with colors including white, black, red, orange, yellow, blue, brown and cream, and metallic gold and silver-white. The most popular category is the Gosanke, made up of the Kōhaku, Taishō Sanshoku and Shōwa Sanshoku varieties. Over 100 varieties exist today, and koi can live over 70 years under optimal conditions. When released into non-native waterways, koi become an [[Invasive species|invasive species]]; their bottom-feeding increases turbidity and displaces native fish.

Jawless fish of the order Petromyzontiformes, with about 38 extant species. Adults have a toothed, funnel-like sucking mouth, an elongated scaleless body and no paired fins. Most of a lamprey's life is spent as a juvenile ammocoete, burrowing into sediment and filter-feeding. Only 18 species are carnivorous, boring into other fish to feed on flesh and blood. Genetic evidence links lampreys to [[Hagfish|hagfish]], the other living group of jawless fish. The sea lamprey, an introduced pest in the [[Great Lakes]], has harmed native fish stocks, and control programs use lampricides and barriers.

Societal collapse in the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, from the late 13th to early 12th century BC. It affected [[Anatolia]], Egypt, the Aegean, eastern [[Libya]] and the [[Balkans]], and it sharply reduced the material wealth of the region's powers. The palace economy of [[Mycenaean Greece]] broke apart into small, isolated village cultures, which were followed by the Greek Dark Ages (c. 1200 to c. 800 BC). The Hittite Empire collapsed, while the [[New Kingdom of Egypt]] survived in weakened form and [[Phoenicia|Phoenicians]] enjoyed increased autonomy. Causes proposed since the 19th century include climate change, droughts, disease, invasions by the [[Sea Peoples]], and changes in military technology that ended chariot warfare. Later research found that many destructions once attributed to the period were misdated or never occurred, so the collapse was more limited than once thought.

State of being free within society from restrictions imposed by authority on one's way of life, behavior, or political views. In U.S. constitutional law, ordered liberty means a balanced society in which individuals can act without unnecessary interference (negative liberty) and have access to opportunities and resources to pursue their goals (positive liberty). Some writers distinguish liberty from freedom, using "freedom" for the ability to do as one wills and "liberty" for the absence of arbitrary restraints, subject to the rights of others. The word comes from [[Latin]] *liber*.

The concept has long occupied philosophers. [[Thomas Hobbes]] held that a free man is one not hindered from doing what he has the will to do. [[John Locke]] rejected that definition: in political society, liberty consists of being under no lawmaking power except that established by consent, and freedom is constrained by laws in both the state of nature and political society. [[John Stuart Mill]]'s *On Liberty* (1859) was the first to recognize the difference between liberty as freedom to act and liberty as absence of coercion. [[Isaiah Berlin]] framed this as the distinction between negative liberty, protection from tyranny and arbitrary authority, and positive liberty, self-mastery over inner compulsions such as weakness and fear. Critics argue that positive liberty can justify coercion in the name of collective goals.

The political concept originates in Greek ideas of freedom and slavery: to be free was not to have a master. [[Aristotle]] linked this to democracy, though it applied only to free men. In the [[Maurya Empire]], citizens of all religions and ethnic groups had some rights to freedom and tolerance. The phrase "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness" appears in the [[United States Declaration of Independence]], and France's motto is "Liberté, égalité, fraternité."

Iron Age kingdom in western [[Anatolia|Anatolia]], with Sardis as its capital and only city, prominent in the 8th to 6th centuries BC. Lydia was known for its wealth in gold and for the world's first coinage; Lydian [[Coin|coins]] made of electrum date to around the 7th century BC and are among the oldest in existence. At its greatest extent in the 7th century BC, it covered all of western Anatolia. In 546 BC it became a satrapy of the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and in 133 BC it became part of the Roman province of Asia. The Lydian language was an [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] language related to Luwian and Hittite, written in an alphabet related to Greek. Sardis's terracing method influenced the planning of other multi-level cities.

16th-century Spanish maritime expedition that was the first to circumnavigate the Earth. It was planned by Portuguese explorer [[Ferdinand Magellan]] to find a western route to the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, because Portugal controlled the eastern route under the 1494 [[Treaty of Tordesillas]]. The five-ship fleet left Spain on September 20, 1519, with about 270 men. It passed through the [[Strait of Magellan]] into the Pacific, which Magellan named Mar Pacifico. Magellan was killed in battle in the Philippines in April 1521, and the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage. Only 18 men and one ship, the *Victoria*, returned to Spain in September 1522. Hardships included [[Scurvy|scurvy]], starvation and mutinies.

Island country in the central [[Mediterranean Sea]] (pop., 2024: 574,250), consisting of Malta, Gozo and Comino. Its capital is [[Valletta]]. Inhabited since at least 6500 BC, Malta was ruled by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and the [[Knights Hospitaller]], who held the islands for 268 years from 1530. It came under British rule as a crown colony in the early 19th century and endured Axis bombing in [[World War II]], for which it was awarded the George Cross.
