Malta gained independence in 1964 and became a republic in 1974. It joined the [[European Union]] in 2004 and adopted the [[Euro]] in 2008. It is a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] and the United Nations. Catholicism is the [[State religion|state religion]], and the economy is now high-income, driven by tourism, financial services and manufacturing.

Systematic method of representing the curved surface of a [[Globe|globe]] on a flat plane. Every projection of a sphere onto a plane distorts the surface in some way, so each one preserves some properties, such as area, shape, direction or distance, at the expense of others. The purpose of the map determines which projection suits it, and the study of projections centers on characterizing their distortions. The best-known is the [[Mercator projection]], which preserves angles but enlarges regions far from the equator; it was criticized through the 20th century and revived in the 21st for online mapping. Equal-area projections, such as the Gall–Peters projection, show the correct sizes of countries relative to one another but distort angles. In September 2026 the [[United Nations]] resolved to promote equal-area projections, notably the Equal Earth projection; 164 countries voted in favor, the [[United States]] voted against, and six abstained.

Latvian-born American abstract painter. He is best known for color field paintings of irregular, painterly rectangles of color, which he produced from 1949 to 1970. Rothko did not subscribe to any one school, though he is associated with the American [[Abstract expressionism|abstract expressionism]] movement. Born into a Jewish family in Daugavpils, Latvia, then part of the [[Russian Empire]], he emigrated to the United States with his family, arriving at [[Ellis Island]] in late 1913 and settling first in [[Portland, Oregon]]. He moved to New York City in 1923. He refunded the Seagram murals commission rather than see the paintings used as decor for wealthy diners, and the Harvard Mural series faded because of the pigment lithol red and sunlight exposure. He contributed 14 canvases to the Rothko Chapel in [[Houston]], Texas. His painting *No. 6 (Violet, Green and Red)* sold in 2014 for $186 million.

Florentine painter regarded as the first great Italian painter of the Quattrocento. He joined the Florentine painters' guild in 1422 and was one of the first artists to use linear [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]] and vanishing points. He moved away from the elaborate ornamentation of the International Gothic style toward a more naturalistic mode, using perspective and chiaroscuro for greater realism. His works include the San Giovenale Triptych and the fresco cycle in the Brancacci Chapel, executed with Masolino in [[Florence]]. Despite a brief career, he influenced many artists, and [[Michelangelo]] studied his frescoes. On hearing of his death, [[Filippo Brunelleschi]] called it a great loss.

American multinational fast-food restaurant chain. Founded in 1940 as a restaurant in San Bernardino, California, by brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald, the company grew under [[Ray Kroc]], a franchise agent who opened a restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois, in 1955 and bought the brothers' stake in 1961. At the end of 2025 the system comprised 45,356 restaurants in more than 100 countries, approximately 95% of them operated by franchisees. Its menu centers on [[Hamburger|hamburgers]] and [[French fries]], including the Big Mac. It directly employed more than 150,000 people, and more than two million others worked at franchised restaurants. The chain has faced criticism over nutrition, treatment of animals, environmental impact and employee wages.

Female monster in [[Greek mythology]], one of the three Gorgons. Medusa was usually described as having living snakes for hair, and anyone who looked at her was turned to stone. Unlike her immortal sisters Stheno and Euryale, she was mortal. The hero Perseus beheaded her with help from [[Athena]], using a mirrored shield to avoid her gaze, and gave the head to Athena, who placed it on her shield. The Gorgons were described by [[Hesiod]] as daughters of the sea gods Phorcys and Ceto, and [[Herodotus]] associated them with Libya. In classical antiquity the image of her head, the Gorgoneion, served as an evil-averting device. Medusa was pregnant by Poseidon when she was beheaded, and the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor sprang from her body.

Family of biomolecules organized as oligomers or polymers, forming the pigments of many organisms. Melanin is produced by melanocytes in a process called melanogenesis, in which the [[Amino acid]] tyrosine is oxidized and then polymerized. There are five basic types: eumelanin, pheomelanin, neuromelanin, allomelanin and pyomelanin. Eumelanin is more abundant in tissues requiring photoprotection, such as the epidermis, and can dissipate over 99.9% of absorbed [[Ultraviolet|UV]] radiation. In human skin, melanogenesis is initiated by UV exposure, which is associated with increased risk of [[Melanoma]]. Pheomelanin is largely responsible for the red or yellow tint of some skin and hair. Neuromelanin, found in the brain, has been studied for possible treatment of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's.

Experiment in 1887 to detect Earth's motion through the luminiferous aether, a medium thought to carry light waves. [[Albert A. Michelson]] and Edward W. Morley compared the speed of light in perpendicular directions at what is now Case Western Reserve University in [[Cleveland]], Ohio. They found no significant difference, a negative result generally considered the first strong evidence against some aether theories. The experiment initiated research that led to [[Special relativity]], which rules out motion against an aether. Later experiments with greater sensitivity found no aether wind; in 2009 optical resonator experiments confirmed its absence at the 10⁻¹⁷ level. Michelson–Morley type experiments were repeated many times with steadily increasing sensitivity and, together with the Ives–Stilwell and Kennedy–Thorndike experiments, form one of the fundamental tests of special relativity.

City (pop., 2011: almost 12.5 million), capital of [[Maharashtra]] state and financial capital of India. Also known as Bombay, it has a deep natural harbor and is the most populous city proper in India; the Mumbai Metropolitan Region has over 20 million people. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, established in 1888, administers the city.

Originally an archipelago of seven islands on the [[Arabian Sea]], it has evidence of human occupation. The [[Maurya Empire]] ruled the islands from the 3rd century BC, and Ptolemy referred to them in AD 150. They were inhabited by the Marathi-speaking Koli people, whose deity Mumbā is believed to have given the city its name. Later the [[Delhi Sultanate]] and the Gujarat Sultanate ruled them. The islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535, transferred to the British Crown in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry, and leased to the [[East India Company]] in 1668. The Hornby Vellard land-reclamation project, begun in 1782 and completed in 1845, unified the islands; with new roads and railways and the 19th-century [[Cotton|cotton]] boom, it made Bombay a major seaport and commercial center. The city played a major role in the [[Indian independence movement]] and became capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

The Government of India officially changed the English name to Mumbai in November 1995, at the insistence of the Shiv Sena party, which argued that "Bombay" echoed British colonial rule. Some residents still use the older name. In the early 2010s the city contributed nearly five percent of India's GDP, one-fourth of its industrial output, and one-third of its tax revenues. It is the center of Bollywood and Marathi cinema.

Branch of science concerned with the description, understanding and prediction of natural phenomena, based on empirical evidence from observation and experimentation. It is divided into two main branches: life science, also known as [[Biology|biology]], and physical science, which includes [[Physics|physics]], [[Astronomy|astronomy]], [[Earth science]] and [[Chemistry|chemistry]]. Natural science succeeded classical [[Natural philosophy|natural philosophy]]. It uses tools from mathematics and logic to convert information about nature into statements of natural laws. Systematic data collection succeeded natural history, which emerged in the 16th century by describing and classifying plants, animals and minerals. Mechanisms such as [[Peer review|peer review]] and reproducibility help ensure the validity of findings. [[Karl Popper]] proposed a controversial criterion of falsifiability to distinguish scientific endeavors from nonscientific ones.

Branch of chemistry concerned with radioactivity and nuclear processes. Its scope covers radioactive elements such as the [[Actinide|actinides]], [[Radium]] and radon, and equipment such as [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]], including corrosion and the behavior of materials in waste storage. It also studies how radiation alters biochemicals in living organisms, which underpins radiation biology and helps explain cancer radiotherapy. Radioactive sources are used in medicine, as industrial and environmental tracers, and to modify materials such as polymers. [[Henri Becquerel]] discovered radioactivity in uranium, and [[Marie Curie]] and Pierre Curie then isolated [[Polonium|polonium]] and radium from uranium ore. [[Ernest Rutherford]] showed that radioactive decay follows a simple equation, implying a characteristic [[Half-life|half-life]].

Splitting of an atomic nucleus into two or more smaller nuclei, releasing large amounts of energy. The process often produces [[Neutron|neutrons]] and [[Gamma ray|gamma rays]]. The fission of one [[Uranium-235]] atom releases about 100 million times the energy of burning one [[Carbon|carbon]] atom in air to produce CO₂. [[Otto Hahn]] and Fritz Strassmann proved in December 1938 that fission had occurred, and [[Lise Meitner]] and Otto Frisch explained it theoretically in January 1939. Hahn and Strassmann predicted additional neutrons, opening the possibility of a chain reaction. Three isotopes, U-233, U-235 and Pu-239, can sustain such a chain reaction, which allows reactors to release energy in a controlled way and weapons to release it uncontrollably within about a microsecond. Most fissions are binary, producing two charged fragments, but three fragments form occasionally (2 to 4 times per 1000 events).

Large [[Biomolecule|biomolecule]] made of nucleotides, essential in all cells and viruses. Each nucleotide consists of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The two main classes are [[DNA]], which contains deoxyribose, and [[RNA]], which contains ribose. The bases are adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil; thymine occurs only in DNA and uracil only in RNA. In DNA, the bases pair in a double helix, with adenine paired to thymine and guanine to cytosine. Sequences of DNA store coded instructions as [[Gene|genes]], and RNA sequences help build the proteins that determine most chemical processes of life. Nucleic acids occur in all life forms, including bacteria, archaea, mitochondria, chloroplasts and viruses. Friedrich Miescher discovered the substance in 1869, and [[Francis Crick]] and [[James Watson]] proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953.

Biochemical and physiological process by which an organism uses food and water to support its life. The intake of these substances provides nutrients, divided into macro- and micronutrients, which are metabolized to create energy and chemical structures; too much or too little of an essential nutrient can cause [[Malnutrition|malnutrition]]. Nutritional science typically emphasizes human nutrition.

The type of organism determines which nutrients it needs and how it obtains them: by consuming organic matter, consuming inorganic matter, absorbing light, or some combination. All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water. Animals require complex nutrients such as [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], [[Lipid|lipids]], and [[Protein|proteins]], obtained by consuming other organisms. Humans developed [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and cooking to replace foraging. Plants acquire nutrients through the soil and atmosphere, and fungi absorb them through the mycelium.

Approximately 30 elements are found in organic matter, with nitrogen, carbon, and phosphorus the most important. Micronutrients, needed in trace amounts, are classified as vitamins (organic) and minerals (inorganic). Essential nutrients are those the body cannot synthesize. Over-nutrition of macronutrients is a major cause of [[Obesity|obesity]] and raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, stroke, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, and some cancers.

Scientific analysis of food began during the chemical revolution of the late 18th century, and modern nutrition science began in the 1910s as micronutrients were identified. Thiamine was the first vitamin chemically identified, in 1926, and in 1932 [[Vitamin C]] was identified as a protection against [[Scurvy|scurvy]]. The first recommended dietary allowances were developed to address fears of deficiency diseases during the Great Depression and the Second World War.

Hardwood tree or shrub of the genus *Quercus* in the [[Beech|beech]] family. Oaks are widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, with some 475 species, both deciduous and evergreen. Each acorn is a [[Nut (fruit)|nut]] borne in a cup. Oaks are keystone species that support more than 950 species of caterpillar and form associations with fungi, including [[Truffle|truffles]]. Their leaves and acorns contain enough [[Tannin|tannin]] to be toxic to cattle. Oak timber is strong and hard, used in construction and [[Furniture|furniture]] making, and oak [[Wine|wine]] barrels age sherry and [[Whisky|whisky]]. Almost a third of oak species are threatened with extinction from [[Climate change|climate change]], pests and habitat loss. The oak is a symbol of strength and the national tree of many countries.

Legendary Greek king of Ithaca and hero of [[Homer]]'s *Odyssey*, known in [[Latin]] as Ulysses. He is the son of Laërtes and Anticlea, husband of Penelope and father of Telemachus, and is renowned for his cunning and resourcefulness, described in Greek as *polytropos*, meaning of many turns. He is most famous for his *nostos*, or homecoming, which took ten years after the decade-long [[Trojan War]]. On the journey he outwits the Cyclops Polyphemus and resists the [[Siren (mythology)|Sirens]]. Back on Ithaca he returns disguised as a beggar to take revenge on suitors who have overrun his palace. Later accounts credit him with devising the [[Trojan Horse]] that led to the fall of [[Troy]].

International organization promoting cooperation among states in the [[Americas|Americas]]. Founded on April 30, 1948, the Organization of American States is headquartered in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D.C.]] and had 32 member states as of November 2023. It is a voluntary body focused on human rights, electoral oversight, social and economic development, and security in the Western Hemisphere. Its origins lie in the First International Conference of American States in 1889-1890, when 18 nations resolved to found the International Union of American Republics. In 1826, [[Simón Bolívar|Simón Bolívar]] and [[José de San Martín|José de San Martín]] proposed a league of American republics at the Congress of Panama, but the resulting treaty was ratified only by [[Gran Colombia|Gran Colombia]]. Albert Ramdin of Suriname became secretary general in May 2025, replacing Luis Almagro of Uruguay.

Series of mountain ranges along the West Coast of [[North America]], from [[Alaska]] to northern and central Mexico. They are part of the North American Cordillera and include the Coast Mountains, Olympic Mountains, Cascade Range and California Coast Ranges. The Insular Mountains of [[Vancouver Island]] lie farther west. In Alaska the ranges contain record-setting tidewater glaciers, while along the coasts of [[British Columbia]] and Alaska the mountains meet the sea in [[Fjord|fjords]] and thousands of islands. In winter, cool air masses from the [[Gulf of Alaska]] bring heavy rain and snow to the ranges north of San Francisco Bay, especially to their western slopes. Plate tectonics shaped the ranges, and the San Andreas fault system in California produces ongoing earthquakes.

Semi-legendary Indian [[Tantra|tantric]] Buddhist master, also known as Guru Rinpoche ("Precious Guru"). Hagiographies credit him with fully revealing [[Vajrayana]] in [[Tibet]], c. 8th–9th centuries. Early Tibetan sources, including the *Testament of Ba*, say he came to Tibet in the 8th century and designed Samye Monastery, the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet, under King Trisong Detsen. With the king and Khenpo Shantarakshita, he is credited with translating the Buddha's teachings and their commentaries into Tibetan, creating the Tibetan Canon. Earlier Tibetologists questioned his historical authenticity, but it is now "cautiously accepted." The Nyingma school regards him as a founding figure. Tibetan Buddhists believe his hidden treasure texts (*termas*) are revealed by *tertöns* (treasure finders). He is widely venerated in Tibet, [[Nepal]], [[Bhutan]], the Himalayan states of India and abroad.

Epidemic of an infectious disease that spreads across a large region, often worldwide. A pandemic involves a sudden increase in cases and affects a substantial portion of the human population. Widespread endemic diseases with stable case numbers, such as seasonal influenza, are generally excluded. The word comes from Greek *pan*, meaning all, and *demos*, meaning people. The [[Black Death]], caused by plague, killed up to half of Europe's population in the 14th century. The 1918 H1N1 influenza pandemic, known as the Spanish flu, is the deadliest in history. More recent pandemics include HIV/AIDS, the 2009 swine flu pandemic and the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. In May 2025 the [[World Health Organization]] adopted a pandemic agreement, approved with 120 votes in favor and 70 abstentions, without the United States, which had withdrawn from the organization.

Act of stopping and leaving a vehicle, usually unoccupied. Parking on one or both sides of a road is often permitted, sometimes with restrictions. Public parking is managed by local government authorities, while private parking is owned by an entity that may restrict it to customers, employees or residents. On-street parking may be parallel, angled or perpendicular, and it can act as inexpensive traffic calming by reducing the effective width of the street. Restrictions may include waiting prohibitions, time limits, payment at a meter, or permit zones. Off-street parking lots and garages are either structured or surface. Cars are typically stationary about 95 percent of the time, and in many North American city centers half or more of all [[Urban area|urban land]] is devoted to car parking. The first public parking garage for motor vehicles was opened in [[Boston]] on May 24, 1898.

Process of preserving foods, such as [[Milk|milk]] and fruit juices, with mild heat. Packaged foods are heated to less than 100 °C (212 °F) to destroy or deactivate [[Microorganism|microorganisms]] and enzymes that cause spoilage or disease, including most vegetative bacteria, though most bacterial spores survive. The process is named after French microbiologist [[Louis Pasteur]], whose research in the 1860s showed that heat could deactivate unwanted microorganisms in wine. It is widely used in the [[Dairy|dairy]] industry. Because the heat is mild, the nutritional quality and taste of treated foods change only slightly. Milk is commonly heated to 72°C for 15 seconds, or to 63°C for 30 minutes. Non-thermal methods such as high-pressure processing and pulsed electric field treatment are also used.

American actress. She made her feature film debut in *A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors* (1987). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for the coming-of-age film *Boyhood* (2014), which was filmed from 2002 until 2014. On television she won a Primetime Emmy Award for the supernatural drama *Medium* in 2005, and another for *The Act* (2019). She has starred in the Apple TV thriller *Severance* since 2022.

Theory and practice of teaching and of the [[Learning|learning]] process. As an academic discipline, pedagogy studies how knowledge and skills are imparted in an educational context, including the interactions between teachers and students. Its most common definition is the study of teaching methods, but some regard it as an art or craft based on tacit knowledge, and others as a catch-all term. Its aims range from liberal education, the general development of human potential, to vocational training in specific skills. Instructive strategies depend on students' background knowledge, their goals and their environment; one example is the [[Socratic method]]. Didactics is usually seen as the narrower term.

Ceremonial capital of the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], in the plains of Marvdasht, Fars province, [[Iran|Iran]]. Encircled by the southern [[Zagros Mountains|Zagros Mountains]], it is a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] World Heritage Site. Its earliest remains date to 515 BC. The complex, raised on a walled platform, included five halls and grand entrances, and was occupied seasonally rather than as a city. Its exact function remains unclear. Most archaeologists long held that it was used for celebrating [[Nowruz|Nowruz]], the Persian New Year, and Iranian nobility and tributary peoples came to present gifts to the king, as shown in the stairway reliefs. In 330 BC the army of [[Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great]] took the complex, and its wooden parts were destroyed by fire. Exploration from the early 17th century led to the rediscovery of [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] writing.

Anthropomorphic figures of death found in many religions and mythologies. In modern stories the Grim Reaper, usually a robed [[Skeleton|skeleton]] with a scythe, collects the soul of the dying. Other beliefs hold that death is a benevolent psychopomp that guides the soul to the [[Afterlife|afterlife]] without controlling when or how a person dies. Death is most often male, but it is female in some cultures, such as Santa Muerte in [[Mexico|Mexico]]. Spanish speakers personify death as female, and the Aztec goddess Mictecacihuatl, "Queen of Mictlan," ruled the underworld. Death is also one of the [[Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse|Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse]]. San La Muerte, a skeletal folk saint, is venerated in [[Paraguay|Paraguay]] and northeast Argentina.

Italian scholar and poet, one of the earliest Renaissance [[Humanism|humanists]]. His rediscovery of [[Cicero]]'s letters is often credited with initiating the 14th-century Italian Renaissance and the founding of Renaissance humanism. In 1345 he discovered a collection of Cicero's letters not previously known to exist, *Epistulae ad Atticum*, in the chapter library of Verona Cathedral. His Latin epic *Africa*, about the Roman general [[Scipio Africanus]], made him a European celebrity, and on April 8, 1341, he was crowned poet laureate on Rome's Capitoline Hill. His *Canzoniere*, a sequence of 366 poems largely inspired by his unrequited love for Laura, established the Petrarchan [[Sonnet|sonnet]] form that influenced European literature for centuries. In the 16th century, Pietro Bembo based the model for modern Italian on Petrarch's works. He is also credited with being the first to develop the concept of the "Dark Ages".

Collection of anonymous Old Norse narrative poems in alliterative verse, known as Eddic poems. The Poetic Edda is distinct from the *Prose Edda* of [[Snorri Sturluson]], and its basis is the medieval Icelandic manuscript *Codex Regius*, also called the Elder Edda. Most poems are in *fornyrðislag* ("old story meter"), with about a quarter in *ljóðaháttr* ("song form"). Like most early poetry, they were passed down orally for centuries. Dating is debated. The poem *Atlamál*, which claims a Greenland origin, must date from about 985 or later, when Scandinavians first reached Greenland. The poems include mythological narratives about gods such as Odin and Thor and heroic lays about legendary figures such as Sigurd. Iceland was settled only around 870, so earlier poems most likely originated in [[Scandinavia]].

Sharp reduction in the size of a [[Population (biology)|population]]. Famines, earthquakes, floods, disease and droughts can cause one, as can human actions such as [[Genocide|genocide]] and intentional culling. The survivors carry less genetic diversity, which weakens the population's ability to adapt to environmental change. [[Genetic drift]] can then fix or eliminate alleles, and [[Inbreeding]] becomes more likely. Bottlenecks are central to conservation biology. North American [[American bison|bison]] fell from approximately 40 million to fewer than 1,000 by the early 1900s through overhunting.

Capital and largest city of [[Rio Grande do Sul]], Brazil, on the eastern bank of the Guaíba Lake. It has about 1.4 million inhabitants (2022) and is the center of Brazil's fifth-largest metropolitan area, with 4.1 million. The official founding date is March 26, 1772, and the city became the provincial capital in 1773. Its port and shipyards grew rapidly in the late 18th century, and it was the first city to implement participatory budgeting. It hosted the World Social Forum in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, and it was a host city for the 2014 [[FIFA]] World Cup and a venue for the 1950 tournament.

City on the Warta River in western [[Poland]], capital of Greater Poland Voivodeship. Poznań is the fifth-largest city in Poland, and its metropolitan area has more than one million inhabitants. One of four historical capitals of medieval Poland, it is an important center of trade, sports, education and tourism, and home to [[Adam Mickiewicz|Adam Mickiewicz University]]. It is the seat of Poland's oldest diocese and hosts the Poznań International Fair, the biggest industrial fair in Poland. Its early stronghold, on what is now Ostrów Tumski, was an important center of the Western Polans, and [[Mieszko I]]'s [[Baptism|baptism]] in AD 966 may have taken place there. In June 1956, workers at the Cegielski factories protested against communist economic policies, and the clashes that followed claimed dozens of lives.

Period of the history of the Americas from the initial peopling of the continents to the onset of European colonization.

The era, also called the pre-contact, pre-Hispanic, or (in Brazil) pre-Cabraline era, runs from the Upper Paleolithic to the voyage of [[Christopher Columbus|Columbus]] in 1492, though in some regions significant European influence came only decades or centuries later. Many Indigenous civilizations developed cities, agriculture, monumental architecture, and complex social hierarchies. Some had declined before the first permanent European colonies and are known mainly through [[Archaeology|archaeological]] research and oral histories; others, such as the [[Maya civilization|Maya]], who kept written records, were documented in European accounts.

Asian Paleo-Indians are thought to have entered the Americas by way of the Bering Land Bridge ([[Bering Strait]]) and possibly along the coast. The date is much debated. The [[Clovis culture]] has sites some 13,000 years old, but sites of 20,000 years have been claimed. A short chronology puts the first movement beyond Alaska no earlier than 14,000–17,000 years ago; a long chronology proposes 30,000–40,000 years ago or earlier.

By the time of contact, populations had diversified into thousands of cultures, estimated at 45–80 million people. Domesticated crops included [[Maize|maize]], potatoes, and quinoa. Major societies included the mound-building Mississippian culture, which built [[Cahokia]]; the Maya, with hieroglyphic writing and calendars; and the [[Inca Empire]] of the Andes, with stonework and roads spanning over 40,000 km. Many of these societies also practiced warfare, slavery, and human sacrifice. North American populations peaked around 1150 before regional declines.

Process for mass reproducing text and images using a master form or template.

The earliest known form evolved from ink rubbings made on paper or cloth from texts on stone tablets in the sixth century, and printing by pressing an inked image onto paper (woodblock printing) appeared later that century. Mechanical woodblock printing on paper began in the 7th century in the [[Tang dynasty]] and spread through East Asia. The first completely surviving printed book is the *[[Diamond Sutra]]* of 868, found at Dunhuang and held in the [[British Library]].

From 900 to 1444 wooden and tin block printing (*ṭarsh*) was used across the Islamic world for amulets, tax receipts, and state decrees, and then vanished without explanation. In [[Europe]], block printing was common on cloth by 1300 and moved quickly to woodcut religious images and playing cards on paper once paper became easily available, around 1400. Block-books, cheaper than manuscripts, emerged in the mid-15th century.

Movable type allowed more flexible processes than hand copying or block printing. Bi Sheng created the first known system in China around 1040, using porcelain. Copper movable type originated in China at the beginning of the 12th century and was used to print Northern Song paper money, though woodblock remained the main method for Chinese, with its thousands of characters. Korea produced the *Jikji* (1377), the earliest extant book printed with metal movable type. [[Johannes Gutenberg]] invented the printing press in the 15th century in Europe, combining cast metal type with a screw press, and the [[Gutenberg Bible]] was printed around 1455.

Printing played a key role in the [[Renaissance]] and the [[Scientific Revolution]] and laid the material basis for the modern knowledge-based economy and the spread of learning to the masses. Methods today include offset lithography for commercial volumes and digital printing for on-demand production.

Condition or claim of an individual or group to be free from unwanted access, observation, or disclosure, and to determine how far they and information about them are exposed to others.

The concept has no single accepted definition. Lawyers, philosophers, and social scientists have understood it as a right to be let alone, as limited access to the self, as secrecy, or as control over personal information.

Distinctions between public and private life appear in many ancient societies, but privacy emerged as a distinct legal claim only in the 19th century, when printing and photographic technologies and the popular press prompted calls for protection. In "The Right to Privacy" (1890), the Boston lawyers Samuel D. Warren and Louis Brandeis argued that the [[Common law|common law]] should recognize a general "right to be let alone". In the second half of the 20th century the spread of computers shifted attention to the collection and processing of personal data, producing data protection law that began in Western Europe in the 1970s and has since spread worldwide.

Privacy is protected as a [[Human rights|human right]] by Article 12 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]], Article 17 of the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]], and regional instruments such as Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. European law tends to treat privacy as an aspect of personal dignity and regulates personal data comprehensively, whereas U.S. law has traditionally emphasized liberty against the state and regulates the private sector by sector.

Privacy overlaps with but differs from [[Security|security]]: information security protects data against unauthorized access, while privacy also concerns whether data should be collected and used at all. The [[Internet]], mobile phones, and large-scale data analysis have intensified debate over [[Surveillance|surveillance]] by governments and corporations. Responses include legislation, litigation, and privacy-enhancing technologies such as [[Encryption|encryption]].

American filmmaker, actor and author. His works are characterized by graphic violence, extended dialogue, [[Profanity|profanity]] and references to [[Popular culture|popular culture]]. His debut feature, the independent crime film *Reservoir Dogs* (1992), was an immediate hit. *Pulp Fiction* (1994) won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] and his first [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]], for Best Original Screenplay, and it was inducted into the National Film Registry of the [[Library of Congress]]. *Kill Bill: Volume 1* (2003) and *Kill Bill: Volume 2* (2004) are regarded as a single film. *Django Unchained* (2012) won him a second Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay, and his later films include *Inglourious Basterds* (2009) and *The Hateful Eight* (2015). His films have grossed more than $1.9 billion worldwide.

Indian actor who works predominantly in Tamil cinema. Born Shivaji Rao Gaikwad, he made his debut in K. Balachander's Tamil drama *Apoorva Raagangal* (1975) and first played antagonists before winning acclaim as a scorned lover in *Bhuvana Oru Kelvi Kuri* (1977). His action film *Billa* (1980), a remake of the [[Hindi]] film *Don*, became his biggest commercial success to that point and gave him an action hero image. He made his Hindi debut with *Andhaa Kaanoon* (1983). Later successes included *Baashha* (1995). *Chandramukhi* (2005) was for a time the highest-grossing Tamil film, and *Enthiran* (2010) and its sequel *2.0* (2018) were India's most expensive productions at the time of their release. He has appeared in about 170 films over more than five decades. The [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 2000 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2016.

Game in which players assume the roles of characters in a fictional setting. Players act out these roles within a narrative, either through literal acting or through structured decision-making about character development, and actions succeed or fail according to formal rules. In the original tabletop form (TTRPG), play is conducted through discussion, and a game master (GM) decides the game system and setting and referees. In live action role-playing (LARP), players physically perform their characters' actions. Electronic forms include multi-user dungeons (MUDs), massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs) and single-player role-playing video games. Tabletop games may also be used in therapy to help people, including young people with neurodevelopmental conditions such as [[Autism|autism spectrum disorders]], ADHD and [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]], develop behavioral, social and language skills.

Ashkenazi Jewish noble banking family originally from [[Frankfurt]], Germany. Mayer Amschel Rothschild, a court factor to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel, established the family's banking business in the 1760s. He passed his wealth to five sons, who set up banks in Paris, Frankfurt, [[London]], [[Vienna]] and [[Naples]]. The family was elevated to noble rank in the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and the [[United Kingdom]]. In the 19th century it held the largest private fortune in the world, and it dominated European finance from the 1820s to the 1870s, when joint-stock banks broke its hegemony. Today its assets span financial services, real estate, mining, energy, agriculture and winemaking. The family has frequently been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories.

Granular material of finely divided rock and mineral particles, usually defined by grain size. Sand grains range from 0.0625 to 2 mm in diameter, smaller than gravel and coarser than silt. Sand can also refer to a soil texture class containing more than 85 percent sand-sized particles by mass. In inland and non-tropical coastal settings its most common constituent is silica (SiO₂), usually as [[Quartz]], which resists weathering. Calcium carbonate dominates in reef areas such as the [[Caribbean]], where it derives from coral and shellfish. Sand is a non-renewable resource over human timescales, and desert sand is unsuitable for [[Concrete|concrete]]; 50 billion tons of beach and fossil sand are used each year for construction.

Gem variety of the mineral [[Corundum|corundum]], consisting of aluminum oxide with trace amounts of iron, titanium, cobalt, chromium and other elements. Blue is the best-known color, but sapphires also occur in yellow, purple, orange, and green, and red corundum is called [[Ruby|ruby]]. The name derives from Latin sapphirus, from Greek sappheiros, which referred to [[Lapis lazuli]]. It scores 9 on the [[Mohs scale]], the third-hardest mineral after diamond and moissanite. Natural sapphires are cut into gemstones for jewelry, and synthetic stones are grown in laboratories. Non-ornamental uses include infrared optical components, high-durability windows, wristwatch crystals and the insulating substrates of [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] and blue LEDs.

Externally threaded [[Fastener|fastener]] tightened or loosened by torque applied to its head. Most screws hold objects together, and the head usually has a slot or other feature that takes a tool such as a screwdriver. Most screws have a right-hand thread. Left-hand threads are used where counterclockwise torque would loosen a right-hand screw, as on the left pedal of a bicycle. The screw first appeared in Mesopotamia during the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC), and Archytas of Tarentum (428–350 BC) described it in Greece. Metal screws were rare in Europe before the 15th century and became common only after machine tools for mass production developed toward the end of the 18th century. The [[Screw mechanism|screw mechanism]] is one of the six classical simple machines defined by Renaissance scientists.

Spiny, globular [[Echinoderm|echinoderm]] forming the class Echinoidea. Approximately 950 species live on the seabed in every ocean, from the intertidal zone to the deep sea. Typically 3 to 10 cm (1 to 4 in) across, they move on hundreds of tube feet and have a rigid test covered in movable spines. Most feed on algae, though they also eat slow-moving animals such as sponges and crinoids. Their predators include sharks, [[Sea otter|sea otters]] and humans. Unchecked by predators, urchins can create barrens devoid of large algae. The fossil record dates from the Ordovician period, some 450 million years ago. Because their embryos are transparent and easy to observe, sea urchins have been a [[Model organism|model organism]] in developmental biology since the 19th century.

Medical disorder that disrupts a person's sleep patterns or sleep quality, with effects on physical, mental and emotional well-being. Sleep disorders are classified by the International Classification of Sleep Disorders into insomnia, sleep-related breathing disorders such as [[Sleep apnea|obstructive sleep apnea]], central disorders of hypersomnolence such as [[Narcolepsy]], circadian rhythm sleep disorders, parasomnias and sleep-related movement disorders. [[Insomnia]], difficulty falling or staying asleep without an obvious cause, is the most common. Contributing factors include increased medication use, age-related changes in [[Circadian rhythm|circadian rhythms]], stress, lifestyle changes and traumatic childhood experiences. Diagnosis commonly uses polysomnography and actigraphy, and sleep disturbances caused by mental, medical or substance abuse disorders should be managed by treating the underlying condition.

Regulations, sanctions, mechanisms, and systems that restrict the behavior of individuals in accordance with social norms and orders. Social control is considered one of the foundations of social order. Sociologists identify two basic forms. Informal control operates through the internalization of norms and values in [[Socialization]], while formal control comprises external sanctions enforced by government to prevent chaos or anomie in society. Some theorists, such as [[Émile Durkheim]], call formal control regulation. Criminal persecutions emerged around the sixth century BC in Athens, Greece, as an early form of formal control. The term was introduced to [[Sociology|sociology]] by Albion Woodbury Small and George Edgar Vincent in 1894. In the 1930s its meaning shifted to an individual's conversion to conformity. It is studied in anthropology, criminology, law, [[Political science|political science]], and sociology.

2001 Japanese animated fantasy film by [[Hayao Miyazaki]], produced by [[Studio Ghibli]]. It follows ten-year-old Chihiro Ogino, who enters a world of kami, the spirits of Japanese [[Shinto]] folklore, after her parents are turned into pigs by the witch Yubaba. She takes a job in Yubaba's bathhouse to free her parents and return to the human world. Distributed in Japan by [[Toho]], the film was released on July 20, 2001, with a budget of US$19 million. It grossed ¥31.68 billion in Japan, the highest-grossing film in Japanese history until 2020, and US$396 million worldwide. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature at the 75th Academy Awards, the first hand-drawn, non-English-language animated film to do so.

American businessman, inventor and investor, and a pioneer of the [[Personal computer|personal computer]] revolution. Jobs co-founded [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] with [[Steve Wozniak]] in 1976 and helped bring the Apple II, one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers, to market. After the board fired him in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought the computer graphics division of Lucasfilm, which became [[Pixar]]. He returned to Apple as chief executive in 1997, when the company was on the verge of bankruptcy, and oversaw products including the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad. The Macintosh 128K of 1984 was the first mass-produced computer with a [[User interface|graphical user interface]].

Mathematical object defined as a family of [[Random variable|random variables]], usually indexed by time. Stochastic processes model systems and phenomena that vary randomly, such as the growth of a bacterial population, electrical current fluctuating from thermal noise, or the movement of a gas molecule. Louis Bachelier used the [[Brownian motion|Wiener process]] to model price changes on the [[Paris]] Bourse, and A. K. Erlang used the Poisson process to model the number of phone calls in a given period. Classes include random walks, martingales, Markov processes, Lévy processes and Gaussian processes. Their study draws on [[Calculus]], [[Linear algebra]] and [[Topology]], and it remains an active field of research.

Need for a drug, the discontinuation of which produces withdrawal symptoms. Also called drug dependence, it is a biopsychological condition in which a person's functioning depends on repeated consumption of a psychoactive substance. Withdrawal, the body's reaction to abstinence, can involve physical symptoms, emotional and motivational symptoms, or both, and it promotes continued use. Dependence potential varies by substance and individual, and dose, frequency, [[Pharmacokinetics|pharmacokinetics]], route of administration, and time are critical factors. Psychological dependence involves gene-expression changes in the nucleus accumbens, where dynorphin reduces [[Dopamine|dopamine]] release. Unlike [[Addiction|addiction]], which is compulsive use despite negative consequences, physical dependence can occur without it. The DSM-5 (2013) merged substance abuse and substance dependence into [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]].

Star at the center of the [[Solar System]], a G-type main-sequence star (G2V) and the main source of energy for life on Earth.

The Sun is a massive sphere of hot plasma, heated to incandescence by [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] reactions in its core, radiating energy from its surface mainly as visible light and infrared radiation, with 10% at ultraviolet energies. It has been an object of veneration in many cultures and a central subject of astronomical research since antiquity. It orbits the [[Galactic Center]] at a distance of 24,000 to 28,000 light-years. Its mean distance from Earth is about 1.496×10⁸ km, or about 8 light-minutes; this distance was used to define the [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]] (au), now defined as 149.5978707×10⁶ km.

The Sun is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System. Its diameter is about 1,391,400 km (864,600 mi), around 109 times that of Earth, and its mass is around 330,000 times Earth's, about 99.86% of the system's total. It has an absolute magnitude of +4.83, estimated to be brighter than about 85% of the stars in the Milky Way, most of which are red dwarfs. It has no definite boundary; its radius is measured to the edge of the photosphere, the apparent visible surface. Its oblateness is 8.2×10⁻⁶, or 8 parts per million, making it the natural object closest to a perfect sphere ever observed. The photosphere is 74.9% hydrogen and 23.8% helium by mass; heavier elements account for less than 2%, chiefly oxygen (roughly 1%), carbon (0.3%), neon (0.2%), and iron (0.2%).

The Sun rotates faster at its equator than at its poles, with a period of approximately 25.6 days at the equator and 33.5 days at the poles relative to the stars, and about 28 days at the equator as seen from Earth. The early Sun rotated up to ten times faster; magnetic braking, as its magnetic field interacted with the outflowing [[Solar wind|solar wind]], slowed it.

The Sun formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a large [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]]; most of the matter gathered in the center, and the rest flattened into a disk that became the Solar System. Every second, its core fuses about 600 billion kg of hydrogen into helium and converts four billion kg of matter into energy. About four to seven billion years from now, as core hydrogen fusion diminishes, the Sun will expand into a [[Red giant|red giant]]. Models suggest it will then shed its outer layers and become a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]], which may glow for perhaps trillions of years before becoming an extremely dense black dwarf. The English word *sun* derives from Old English *sunne*; the adjective *solar* comes from Latin *sol*. The astronomical symbol is ☉.

Device that tells the time of day from the position of the Sun's shadow on a marked dial. In its narrowest sense it consists of a flat dial plate and a gnomon, whose shadow aligns with hour lines as the Sun moves across the sky. The style, the time-telling edge of the gnomon, must be parallel to Earth's axis for accuracy throughout the year, and its angle from horizontal equals the sundial's [[Latitude|latitude]]. Sundials show local solar time, so clock time requires corrections for the equation of time, which can be as great as 16 minutes, 33 seconds, and for the difference between the local [[Longitude|longitude]] and that of the official [[Time zone|time zone]]. Forms include horizontal, vertical, equatorial, polar and analemmatic dials. The earliest known examples date to ancient Egypt around 1500 BCE.

Ruler of the [[Khmer Empire]] (r. 1113–1150). He is best known as the builder of [[Angkor Wat]], the largest Hindu temple in the world, which he dedicated to Vishnu and [[Shiva]]. Reaching the throne through a contest with rival claimants, he reunited the empire, and vassals paid him tribute. His monumental architecture, military campaigns and restoration of strong government have led historians to rank him among the empire's greatest rulers. He sent a mission to the [[Chola dynasty]] of south India and presented a precious stone to Chola Emperor Kulothunga Chola I in 1114. His eastern campaigns against [[Champa]] were largely unsuccessful, although in 1145 he appears to have invaded it and sacked its capital, Vijaya. The first syllables of his name are a [[Sanskrit]] root meaning *sun*.

Ancient geometric symbol used in many cultures and religions across [[Eurasia]]. Its name comes from the Sanskrit *svastika*, meaning "conducive to well-being." In [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]] it is a sacred symbol of good luck, prosperity and auspiciousness. It was seen as auspicious in much of the Western world until the 1930s. It was first used as an international symbol of [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] by the Romanian politician A. C. Cuza before [[World War I]]. After the German [[Nazi Party]] adopted it as an emblem of the so-called Aryan race, it appeared on the flag of [[Nazi Germany]]. Several countries prohibit displaying it by law, with exceptions for religious symbolism, and it remains a symbol of good luck in Asian Hindu, Buddhist and Jain communities.

Country in [[West Asia]] on the eastern Mediterranean, officially the Syrian Arab Republic. [[Damascus]] is the capital and largest city, and the population is about 26 million. After centuries of [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] rule, Syria was a French mandate and gained de jure independence in 1945 and de facto independence in 1946. Coups were frequent until a 1963 coup established one-party rule by the Ba'ath Party. Hafez al-Assad came to power in 1970, and his son [[Bashar al-Assad]] succeeded him in 2000. The [[Syrian civil war]] began in 2011 and culminated in the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. [[Ahmed al-Sharaa]] was formally appointed president in January 2025. Levantine Arabs are the largest ethnic group and Sunni Muslims the largest religious group. The economy, once mainly agricultural, deteriorated after 2011, and the country has six UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Person who helps students acquire knowledge, competence or virtue through [[Teaching|teaching]]. Teachers are also called schoolteachers or educators. Anyone may take on the role informally, but in most countries formal teaching in [[School|schools]] and colleges is done by paid professionals. Duties include preparing lessons according to agreed [[Curriculum|curricula]], giving lessons and assessing pupil progress. Teachers may instruct in [[Literacy|literacy]] and numeracy, vocational skills, the [[The arts|arts]], religion, civics or life skills. They have a legal duty to protect students from harm, such as bullying and abuse. The required competences vary by culture, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has argued for a shared definition of what teachers need to know and do.

Transmission of information over a distance by electrical or electronic means, typically through cables, radio waves, or other technologies. Channels may be divided for multiplexing, letting one medium carry several concurrent sessions. Long-distance technologies of the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries generally use electric power and include the electrical telegraph, [[Telephone|telephone]], [[Television|television]], and [[Radio|radio]]. The term was coined in 1904 by the French engineer and novelist Édouard Estaunié, who defined it as "remote transmission of thought through electricity". Slow methods such as postal mail are excluded from the definition.

Earlier methods included smoke signals, beacons, and homing pigeons; in 1849 Paul Julius Reuter ran a pigeon service carrying stock prices between Aachen and Brussels until the telegraph gap closed. In 1792 Claude Chappe built the first fixed visual telegraph line, between Lille and Paris; the last commercial line was abandoned in 1880. On July 25, 1837, William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone demonstrated the first commercial electrical telegraph. [[Samuel Morse]] independently developed a version and a code that was an important advance. Many inventors contributed to the telephone, including [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. [[Guglielmo Marconi]], who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics, led a revolution in wireless communication in the first decade of the 20th century.

Since the 1960s, digital technologies have supplemented voice with data, and the limits of metallic media prompted optical fiber. Mobile networks evolved from 1G analog to 5G. The [[Internet]] is independent of any given medium and has widened global access to services. In the United States, the AT&T monopoly was broken up in 1984; debates persist over natural monopoly in network deployment and the need for antitrust oversight.

Oil-on-canvas painting by Dutch Post-Impressionist [[Vincent van Gogh]], painted in June 1889. It depicts the view from the east-facing window of his room at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just before sunrise, with an imaginary village added. Van Gogh had voluntarily admitted himself to the asylum in May 1889 and produced many paintings during his year-long stay. The celestial elements include [[Venus]], visible at the time, and a Moon whose depiction is not astronomically accurate. Scientific analysis has confirmed Van Gogh's use of [[Ultramarine|ultramarine]] and cobalt blue for the sky. The painting has been held by the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in New York City since 1941, acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest. It has been described as a "touchstone of modern art."

[[Ancient Greece|Ancient Greek]] theatrical culture that flourished from 700 BC. At its center was [[Athens]], where theater was institutionalized as part of the Dionysia festival honoring the god [[Dionysus]]. [[Tragedy|Tragedy]], comedy and the satyr play emerged there as the three dramatic genres; tragedy is dated to the late 500 BC and comedy to 490 BC. The festival was possibly organized to foster loyalty among the tribes of Attica, and it was created around 508 BC. Athens exported the festival to its numerous colonies. Modern Western theater borrows from this tradition its technical terminology, genre classification, and many of its themes, stock characters and plot elements.

British polymath. Young made notable contributions to vision, light, solid mechanics, energy, physiology, language, musical harmony and Egyptology. He is credited with establishing [[Christiaan Huygens]]' wave theory of light, in contrast to the corpuscular theory of [[Isaac Newton]]. In 1801 he proposed a trichromatic theory of color vision and identified astigmatism, and in 1807 he formulated [[Young's modulus]], a measure of a material's stiffness. In 1814 he deciphered the demotic script of the [[Rosetta Stone]] and identified phonetic values in hieroglyphs. His work influenced [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], [[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[Albert Einstein]]. Young also practiced as a physician and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1794.

Tall structure, taller than it is wide, built to serve purposes other than habitation. Towers are distinguished from masts by their lack of guy-wires and, like tall buildings, are self-supporting. Height serves functions such as clock visibility, surveillance from a [[Castle|castle]], observation, leisure and telecommunications. The oldest known may be a circular stone tower in the walls of Neolithic Jericho (8000 BC). Ziggurats, such as the Sumerian [[Ziggurat of Ur]] built in the 3rd millennium BC, were among the earliest towers. The Chinese used towers as part of the [[Great Wall of China]] in 210 BC during the [[Qin dynasty]], and medieval fortified buildings made wide use of them. Modern examples include the [[Eiffel Tower]] in Paris, completed in 1889 as a temporary entrance arch for the World's Fair, and [[Cooling tower|cooling towers]] at industrial plants.

Italian medievalist, philosopher, [[Semiotics|semiotician]] and novelist, best known for *The Name of the Rose* (1980). Born in Alessandria, Piedmont, he wrote his thesis on the aesthetics of [[Thomas Aquinas]] at the University of Turin and later taught for much of his life at the [[University of Bologna]]. His 1980 historical mystery combined semiotics, biblical analysis and medieval studies, and *Foucault's Pendulum* (1988) explored the history of occultism. From 1985 he wrote a twice-monthly column, *La Bustina di Minerva*, for the magazine *L'Espresso*. His 1995 essay "Ur-Fascism" lists fourteen properties of [[Fascism|fascist]] ideologies. His *A Theory of Semiotics* (1975) became a foundational text in the field.

Substance in the [[Gas|gas]] phase at a [[Temperature|temperature]] below its critical temperature, so that it can be [[Condensation|condensed]] to a [[Liquid|liquid]] by increasing pressure alone. A vapor may coexist with its liquid or solid phase in equilibrium, and the vapor pressure of a liquid or solid is its equilibrium pressure at a specific temperature. Water vapor condenses into [[Fog|fog]] and clouds when its partial pressure is raised enough. Vapor is central to evaporation and [[Distillation|distillation]]. A vapor differs from an [[Aerosol|aerosol]], which is a suspension of tiny particles of liquid or solid in a gas. Mercury-vapor and sodium-vapor lamps produce light from atoms in excited states.

Chinese poet, painter, musician and statesman of the middle [[Tang dynasty]]. He is regarded as one of the most distinguished figures in Chinese arts and letters, renowned for his dual talents as a nature poet and landscape painter. About 400 of his poems survived, and 29 are included in the 18th-century anthology *Three Hundred Tang Poems*. No authenticated paintings survive, and none of his music is preserved. Born into an aristocratic family, he passed the palace examination in 721 with top place and first served as a court musician. He was demoted to overseeing a granary in the former province of Jizhou, now in [[Hebei]]. Later he was posted to the frontier at Liangzhou. Late in life he became a devout Chan Buddhist and a vegetarian. His poems were compiled at imperial command by his brother Wang Jin.

Flowering plant of the [[Cucurbitaceae]] family, grown worldwide for its large fruit. The watermelon (*Citrullus lanatus*) is a scrambling, vine-like plant whose fruit is a large [[Berry (botany)|berry]] with a firm rind and no internal divisions. Its sweet, juicy flesh is usually deep red to pink, with many seeds that are black when mature. The modern watermelon originated in [[Sudan]], where it was first domesticated, and it was cultivated in Egypt by 2000 BC. Dessert watermelons spread around the Mediterranean during Roman antiquity. Breeding has produced disease-resistant and seedless [[Cultivar|cultivars]] that bear mature fruit within 100 days of planting. In 2024, China produced 60% of the world's watermelons. The fruit is eaten raw or made into juice or wine, and the rind is edible when pickled or cooked. The sweet watermelon was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.

Triangular [[Tool|tool]], a portable [[Inclined plane|inclined plane]] and one of the six [[Simple machine|simple machines]]. It separates objects, lifts them or holds them in place by converting force applied to its blunt end into forces perpendicular to its inclined surfaces. Its mechanical advantage is the ratio of its slope length to its width, equal to 1/tan α for tip angle α, so a smaller angle gives a greater lifting force. Wedges have existed for thousands of years; the hand axe, made by chipping flint, may be the first example. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptian]] quarries used [[Bronze|bronze]] wedges to split blocks of stone, as well as wooden wedges that swelled when soaked with water. Wedges split wood along the grain, and a narrow gib finely adjusts distances in machine tools. The tips of forks and [[Nail (fastener)|nails]] also act as wedges, and a blade is a compound inclined plane.

Distilled [[Liquor|liquor]] made from fermented grain mash, usually [[Barley]], corn, [[Rye]] or [[Wheat]]. It is typically aged in charred white [[Oak|oak]] casks, and all classes share grain fermentation, distillation and aging in wooden casks. The name is an anglicization of the Gaelic word *uisce*, meaning "water"; the spelling whiskey is common in [[Ireland]] and the [[United States]]. Scotch whisky must be distilled and matured in oak casks in [[Scotland]] for at least three years. In the United States, bourbon must contain at least 51% corn in its mash. It is one of the world's most popular spirits, and Scotch exports were valued at £5.4 billion as of 2024.

Free online encyclopedia written and maintained by volunteer editors. It was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001 as a [[Wiki|wiki]] complement to Nupedia, an expert-written encyclopedia project. It has been hosted since 2003 by the Wikimedia Foundation, an American nonprofit funded mainly by reader donations. It is the largest and most read reference work in history. As of November 2026 the English edition has more than seven million articles, and all editions together exceed 68 million. Its reliability was often criticized in the 2000s but has earned more praise since the late 2010s. Critics point to systemic [[Bias|bias]], including gender bias against women and geographic bias against the Global South. Some national governments have censored it, from specific pages to the entire site.

Iraqi-born British architect and designer. Hadid was born in [[Baghdad]] and studied mathematics at the American University of Beirut before enrolling in 1972 at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in [[London]]. She adopted painting as a design tool and abstraction as a method, drawing on Suprematism and the Russian avant-garde. Her major works include the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics, the Broad Art Museum, Rome's MAXXI Museum and the Guangzhou Opera House. She was the first woman to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize, in 2004, and won the Stirling Prize in 2010 and 2011. In 2012 [[Elizabeth II]] made her a Dame for services to architecture. [[The Guardian|The Guardian]] called her the "Queen of Curves". Several buildings, including the Daxing International Airport in [[Beijing]], were still under construction at the time of her death.

City in central [[Poland]] and capital of Łódź Voivodeship, a former industrial center (pop., 2025: 639,890). Granted town rights in 1423 by King [[Władysław II Jagiełło]], it was annexed by Prussia in the Second Partition of 1793 and joined Congress Poland, a Russian client state, after the [[Congress of Vienna]] in 1815. Rapid growth in [[Textile|textile]] manufacturing from 1850 drew migrants, including many Jews and Germans, which made the city multinational. The Muzeum Sztuki, founded in 1931, was the first museum in Europe dedicated to collecting and showcasing modern art. During [[World War II]] the German occupiers forced the city's large Jewish minority into a walled ghetto before sending its members to German concentration and extermination camps. After a sharp decline following 1989, the city began to revitalize its downtown in the 2010s. Its National Film School is a cradle for many of Poland's most renowned actors and directors, and in 2017 the city was named a [[UNESCO]] City of Film.
